title: Bond Girl Lea Seydoux Says ‘I Don’t Really Care’ Who Becomes 007’s New Female Lead: ‘It’s Become American’ Now
full_text: × Nov 19, 2026 10:04am PT Bond Girl Lea Seydoux Says ‘I Don’t Really Care’ Who Becomes 007’s New Female Lead: ‘It’s Become American’ Now By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Penelope Cruz to Star in and Produce Netflix Drama ‘Patricia’ From ‘On the Fringes’ Director Juan Diego Botto 7 hours ago YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content 7 hours ago Netflix Eyes Return to Cannes After 10 Years as Festival Lobbies for Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ Starring Josh O’Connor 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Piccolo America While the news of Robert Pattinson ‘s casting as the new James Bond has sparked a frenzy on social media, Léa Seydoux, who starred opposite Daniel Craig in two James Bond movies, has little interest in finding out who will play the next Bond girl. Speaking on a recent episode of The Runthrough podcast which was recorded before Pattinson was announced as the new OO7, Seydoux was asked who she thought should play the next Bond girl, or Bond woman. “I don’t really care,” she said, laughing. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?” Related Stories Queen Latifah, Bone Thugs-N-Harmony, MC Lyte and More to Lead 2027 Rock the Bells Cruise Seydoux, who played Madeleine Swann in “Spectre” and “No Time to Die,” said Amazon MGM Studios’ takeover of the franchise signaled a “new era.” “It became American. But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve , who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great,” she said. Seydoux previously told Variety in an interview before the Cannes Film Festival that she “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.” Seydoux, who worked Villeneuve on “Dune: Part 2,“ also revealed that she had sent Villeneuve a note congratulating him on his appointment. “He’s super cultured — he knows so much about cinema, but not only cinema,” she told Variety . The actor, who’s a contender in the 2027 Oscar race with “Gentle Creature” and “The Unknown,” also weighed in on the search for Craig’s successor as the iconic British spy. “It’s really difficult to cast James Bond, because you need to find an actor with a depth and with many layers, and I don’t think that the young generation really has that,” she said on the podcast. Seydoux’s character played a pivotal role in Craig’s final Bond outing, “No Time to Die,” which ended with the spy sacrificing himself to save Madeleine and their daughter. The French actor, who broke out internationally with Abdellatif Kechiche’s Palme d’Or-winning “Blue Is the Warmest Colour,” has worked with famed international auteurs including Wes Anderson, David Cronenberg and Yorgos Lanthimos. title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV
full_text: × Nov 19, 2026 10:00am PT ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV Tarantino and David Fincher merge in a divertingly odd way. The film hops from one thing to the next, but it's disarmingly placid and even-keeled. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Madden’ Review: Nicolas Cage Plays John Madden as the Disheveled Buddha of Football in David O. Russell’s Eccentric Stunt of a Sports Biopic 2 days ago ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: Not as Deadly as ‘Songbirds & Snakes,’ the Haymitch Origin Story Makes for a Watchable if Meandering Prequel 2 days ago ‘The Gospel of Christmas’ Review: Tyler Perry’s Churchy Musical Drama Does a Threadbare Job of Getting Into the Spirit 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection “ The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth ” gives you a highly pleasurable, shaggy heat-of-the-moment buzz. I’m not sure what I was expecting from a sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” but I dug just about every ambling, low-down minute of this one. (I realize that low-down is an ancient phrase, but this is a movie that ends with Boz Scaggs’ “Lowdown” playing over the closing credits. That’s how 1977 it is.) The film is Quentin Tarantino , who wrote the screenplay, going wherever the day (or night) takes him. And that will do just fine. But it’s also Tarantino honed and manicured, given a polish of precision by the film’s director, David Fincher . As an artist, the hot-blooded, motormouth Tarantino is Dionysian; the rigorously controlled, ice-in-his-veins Fincher is Apollonian. Together, the two merge in a divertingly odd way. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is an enjoyable contradiction — a meticulous hangout movie. It hops from one thing to the next, but it’s disarmingly placid and even-keeled about what it’s doing. In spirit, it’s almost as if someone had slipped the movie half a Quaalude. It’s got no worries, and neither does its hero, Cliff Booth ( Brad Pitt ), the most sexy-cool aging ex-stuntman you’ll ever see. Related Stories Queen Latifah, Bone Thugs-N-Harmony, MC Lyte and More to Lead 2027 Rock the Bells Cruise “The Further Mis-Adventures” sprawls over one week in Los Angeles in the latter half of ’77 (the specificity has meaning; it’s supposed to be just after “Star Wars” has changed the force of the movie universe), and the tone is less sunlit intense than the 1969 of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The counterculture has now evaporated, and everyone is stuck in a lackadaisical limbo of diversion, with one foot in the past. That doesn’t mean “The Further Mis-Adventures” is snobbish about the pop-culture era it’s rooted in. The film is brazenly and ever-so-slightly-ironically approving, whether it’s reveling in the throb of disco or the grand orchestral pomp of ELO’s “Tightrope,” smacking its lips at a tacky margarita bar that features mud-wrestling night, or opening with a last-days-of-blaxploitation movie called “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” in which a couple of mack daddies sit around talking about the libidinous challenge of keeping their stables happy. There’s a trick that Tarantino and Fincher spring several times here, and that’s to lure us into a piece of entertainment — a movie, a TV show — as if it were actually happening. That’s their tribute to the canny power of this stuff. Yet even as “The Further Mis-Adventures” embraces all this, you can feel a certain what’s-next? affectlessness hanging in the smoggy air. The only one who doesn’t feel it is Cliff, who lives in the eternal present. You might say that Cliff has become something of a loser. His old buddy Rick Dalton, who kept him supplied with stunt-double work, is now history (Rick has moved to Australia), and Cliff, with a slight limp and aching joints, is a man pushing 50, living with his cranky pawn-shop-owner dad (Peter Weller) in Marina del Rey, working odd jobs, driving around in his muscle-car jalopy. Yet in his slightly grizzled way he’s still a dreamboat, not to mention the most comfortable man in his own skin God ever invented. Bringing Cliff back and expanding him into a more central presence, Brad Pitt hits the aura jackpot. With a Redford mustache and killer grin and golden sweep of honey-blond hair, parading around in gaudy short-sleeve bartender shirts with three or four buttons open, he makes Cliff high on his own supply of flinty good vibes. Cliff takes whatever comes at him, and that’s a life that suits him fine. He’s chivalrous and polite, but that’s connected to how comfortable he is with violence. He has no anxiety about it, and no anxiety about anything else. Pitt takes his own slightly seedy movie-star nobility and turns it up to full irresistible throttle. Even his voice is yummy — the sandy baritone directness of it, with that hint of a SoCal drawl. His Cliff puts everyone at ease, including the audience, but he keeps you guessing because he’s a paradox: a himbo with brains who can read anyone in the room — a sexy cowboy handyman who, if need be, will cut your throat. The film’s opening episode is an appetizer of violence. It’s Tuesday night, and Cliff is working his shift as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema (the first of the film’s Tarantino Easter-egg in-jokes — there will be more, including a TV commercial for Red Apple cigarettes featuring Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate). The theater is showing “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” and Cliff talks along with some of the tastier dialogue as he changes reels. But his real job comes after the theater closes. That’s when he has to rendezvous with a scurvy thief (Karren Karagulian), who has brought along the twink hustler (Corey Fogelmanis) he picked up on Santa Monica Boulevard. The thief is looking to fence some items he stole from a house in the Hollywood Hills. But the robbery victim, unbeknownst to him, is one of Cliff’s old director pals. In short order, Cliff gets rid of the thief and puts the hustler on a bus back to Ohio. The shock — and joke — of it is that Cliff kills a man as casually as if he were mixing a banana margarita on his bartending night. That’s the Zen of Cliff Booth. Fincher has referred to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” as “‘Shampoo’ with violence” (an ace description), and that’s to say: It’s all about Cliff drifting around. It isn’t necessarily trying to be a movie story. But the film is fixated on Hollywood, to the point that each new location is identified with an onscreen title that will say (for instance) “Beverly Hills, 4.3 miles west of Hollywood,” as if Hollywood were the nucleus of the universe. What’s telling about “Cliff Booth” is that in its random anecdotal hangout way, it’s actually rooted in the world of television. Rick moved to Australia because he’s starring in a TV series there called “Dingo Dan.” Those items stolen by the thief include a best director Oscar statuette, which implies that that trophy is a relic of a lost age. And the plot of “The Further Mis-Adventures” centers on Cliff getting summoned by Charlie Peters ( Scott Caan ), a garishly obnoxious star of TV Westerns and combat series. Charlie, who thinks he knows everything, does all his own stunt work (which suggests the character might be a Tarantino tweak of Tom Cruise — though the two characters, aside from being of average height, don’t have much else in common). Charlie, though, needs Cliff for something else: to get him out of an underworld jam. This is, after all, the stuntman who beat up Bruce Lee. So Cliff meets with Charlie’s agent, the imperially tall, British, and coldly sexy Kate Crosby ( Elizabeth Debicki ). These two get a flirtation going — one so frosty that in spirit it feels more 2026 than 1977. You can see that there’s a mutual attraction. And you really see it after Cliff confesses his feelings, and their gamesmanship turns weirdly kinky. (The weird part is that the kink stays so casual.) But she’s classy and standoffish, and the most revealing conversation the two have is about the movies. It’s one of those freewheeling Tarantino digressions (built on what sounds like a scrap from his abandoned script for “The Critic”), in which Kate tells Cliff that she was briefly a film critic who had gotten to know Pauline Kael (who Cliff dismisses because she didn’t like “Butch Cassidy”). Kate, sounding like a corrupt studio executive, says she now thinks of movies strictly as entertainment, and never as art. Cliff asks: Even “The Godfather”? Yes, she says, that’s just a gangster movie with artistic airs. It’s strange that the film never counters this view; it’s almost as if Tarantino agrees with it. Has he gone that far into pulp fetishization? (The author of “Cinema Speculation” is actually a great critic.) Or maybe he’s saying: Now that “Star Wars” has arrived, the movies as we knew them are dead. I’m going on about this because I think it helps explain the enjoyably random, slightly disjunctive air of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” It’s the first Tarantino film that feels, in its structural DNA, like a glorified television series. At one point, the movie was supposed to be a series, and in spirit that’s kind of what it still is. Call it QT TV. The incidents hook you, but with less consequence than they’d have in a full-blown, let-it-rip Tarantino movie. “The Further Mis-Adventures” looks like a movie (Fincher gives it a stately sheen), and it’s way too violent for television. But the hangout factor, in this case, feels one small step removed from the characters-on-a-TV-series-are-your-family factor. Driving the action forward are a pair of Filipino hitmen, the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), who are singular in their viciousness; one employs a scary hatchet he calls Esmerelda. Scott Caan does a blustery job of playing Charlie, the blowhard TV star (I enjoyed the scene where he uses a live round of ammunition to put the fear into Timothy Olyphant as a fellow actor playing a Nazi), but given how central the character is, I wish he were less of a putz. I also wish we didn’t have to watch Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II), Charlie’s football-player-turned-actor costar, get not simply beat up but maimed for no good reason. On the other hand, I appreciated the quick reference to Cliff doing porn, which becomes a punchline to the fact that everyone he meets feels like they’ve seen him before. Speaking of porn, there’s a shoutout/tweak to PTA when “Best of My Love,” the Emotions track that opens “Boogie Nights,” comes on the car radio and Cliff flips the channel. How is the ultraviolent climax? It’s kind of spectacular. Tarantino doesn’t use it to rewrite history this time, but in a funny way he does an instant mini version of that. What happens to Cliff in the big fight at the end should, by all rights, have eliminated him from the earth. But it doesn’t. It’s just a scratch. He doesn’t give a fuck, and he’s still there. To put it in QT TV terms: When’s the next episode? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV Reviewed at AMC Empire, New York, Nov. 17, 2026. title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt, David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino Mix a Cool Cocktail in Free-Flowing Spinoff
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All November 19, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt and Elizabeth Debicki in 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.' Courtesy of Netflix It’s difficult to imagine a song choice more precisely capturing the essence of a movie than Boz Scaggs’ mellow yacht rock groove “Lowdown,” which kicks off the end credits of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . That might seem odd for a gritty comedy that builds to an ultraviolent climactic bloodbath, but this standalone chapter in the life of the now-retired stuntman from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood — the role that won Brad Pitt an Oscar — saunters along to its own idiosyncratic beat, running on a well-lubricated R&B engine. The star’s golden glow and loose-limbed charisma, David Fincher ’s exactingly controlled direction and the shaggier storytelling style of Quentin Tarantino ’s screenplay are not always the most seamless fit. But the obvious mutual esteem and affection shared by that creative triumvirate is contagious and the movie has a good-time vibe that just won’t quit — even if it feels more stretched and less substantive than its 2019 predecessor. Still, few fans will complain, especially those who opt for the IMAX experience, before it hits Netflix on Dec. 23. Related Stories Movies Ron Howard Wasn't Sure He Was the Right Director for 'Avedon'; This Is What Changed His Mind TV Netflix to Adapt 'Grendel' Comic Books Into Adult Animated TV Series The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth The Bottom Line Sexy, seductive and chaotic in mostly fun ways. Release date : Weds., Nov. 25 (in theaters); Weds., Dec. 23 (streaming) Cast : Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis, Karren Karagulian, Lauren Glazier, Timothy Olyphant, Nicholas Hammond Director : David Fincher Screenwriter : Quentin Tarantino Rated R, 2 hours 23 minutes Eight years have passed since Cliff and Leonardo DiCaprio’s faded TV star Rick Dalton, for whom Pitt’s character worked as a longtime stunt double, mopped up three homicidal Manson followers — described here as “those fuckin’ hippie intruders” — in pools of their own blood. Rick is now starring in a TV series in Australia drolly titled Dingo Dan , and Cliff has aged out of the stunt game, though his is not an idle retirement. He works as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema — the historic repertory house in the Fairfax district now owned and programmed by Tarantino as a 35mm stronghold — where the fictional blaxploitation film Soul Brothers Die Hard has been such a hit that Cliff can recite the dialogue along with the actors. Its cast is topped by former Oakland Raiders player Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison ( Yahya Abdul-Mateen II ), who opens Fincher’s film with a quintessential Tarantino provocation, enlightening his character’s nephew about “how to keep multiple bitches turnt out.” Cliff also mixes killer cocktails at a rowdy Redondo Beach tiki bar that features female mud-wrestling contests and picks up occasional work as “a day player” on XXX porn movies, including one currently in production titled The Sexorcist . For recreation, he participates in punishing demolition derby meets. But Cliff’s main source of off-the-books income is as a fixer operating outside the law to solve problems for rich Angelenos in a jam. One task he’s assigned is to retrieve jewelry and a best director Oscar stolen from a married Hollywood veteran by Joey (Corey Fogelmanis), the young hustler he picked up outside Astro Burger on Santa Monica Blvd. When Joey shows up at the New Beverly with criminal associate Chicken Hawk (Sean Baker favorite Karren Karagulian) to exchange the goods for a wad of cash, Cliff turns the transaction to his advantage with brisk decisiveness and zero conscience. Pitt’s Cliff in Once Upon a Time was very much a sidekick, a laid-back man of few words compared to Rick. This time around, he’s become a much more loquacious operator. But the film’s episodic nature — jumping around in time and neighborhood, shifts marked in onscreen text — makes the early action ambling and discursive. It takes an inordinate amount of time to settle on a central plot thread. Is it a romance? A crime thriller? A dark comedy? A hangout movie whose foremost concern is nostalgic time travel to late ‘70s Los Angeles? Actually, it’s all those things, though it can feel unfocused. The narrative wheels kick into gear when Cliff gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby ( Elizabeth Debicki , never better), whose TV star client Charlie Peters ( Scott Caan ) has requested a meeting. Given that Charlie is known for doing all his own stunts — a detour into his career highlights shows B&W footage from popular series with titles like Fireball Jungle , Tom Horn: Stock Detective and Enemy Territory , along with an appearance on the Johnny Carson show — Cliff is perplexed as to the purpose of the meeting and Karen is unforthcoming with details. It’s likely she hasn’t even been let in on what Charlie wants. Meanwhile, a pair of gangster brothers in town from the Philippines for a job, Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), start making their presence felt, first with a jolt of horrific violence when they break into a family’s home in an upscale neighborhood. Even by Tarantino’s standards the brutal ugliness of that incident is shocking, made even more vicious by Eddie’s weapon of choice, a massive hammer he calls Esmarelda. It turns out Charlie partied hard with the Verduscos while shooting in the Philippines, coincidentally where Cliff served in World War II, while the country was under Japanese occupation. On a drunken impulse, Charlie hired the brothers to eliminate a problem and although he has tried to back out of the deal, they have come to follow through and collect. That puts the TV star, Cliff and even Hot Rod in danger, since he and Charlie are shooting a private eye TV movie called Disco Kingpin . There’s an Elmore Leonard kinship in the crime elements; Fincher takes his cue from Tarantino by making us squirm and laugh through even the most sadistic acts. But the movie lavishes just as much time and attention on Cliff’s slow-burn romancing of Karen and his playful banter with Charlie’s wife Toni ( Carla Gugino ), with whom he had a fling — unbeknownst to Charlie — while they were working on a Rick Dalton dud titled Salty the Talking Sea Otter . A tennis club doubles match with Cliff and Karen playing Charlie and Toni is key to establishing the latter’s significance in a tricky scenario to be revealed. It’s no surprise that Cliff takes charge of Charlie’s predicament, never losing his cool even when he’s seriously at risk. As much as the movie is enamored with L.A., its period landmarks and the usual load of pop-culture ephemera so beloved by Tarantino, it’s also a big fat valentine to guys like Cliff, chill dudes cut from the same cloth as Steve McQueen. The film is more driven by casual vignettes than complex action set pieces, even if the spectacularly bloody final act is up there with Tarantino’s most operatic explosions of violence. Often, The Further Mis-Adventures is so busy swooning over Brad/Cliff that it plays like episodic TV or part of a pulpy paperback series built around the lovable reprobate character. It’s less robust as a feature-length narrative, though that doesn’t make it any less entertaining. Tarantino disciples will eat it up, while Fincher obsessives should find plenty of the director’s pungent atmospherics, his technical flair and moody visual style. Cliff’s inevitable showdown with the Verduscos seems not so much a story in its own right as a chapter in the man’s personal mythology to go along with the legends that Charlie recaps with breathless hero worship — notably that time he took down Bruce Lee. Tarantino doubles down on that here, thumbing his nose at the many people who found his irreverent besmirching of the martial arts icon insulting. Caan is doing some of his best work, amusingly bouncing Charlie’s excitability off Cliff’s relaxed stoner gestalt or Karen’s self-possessed composure. For once using her native accent and taking full advantage of her imposing height, Debicki is in sublime command of her powers playing a savvy, languidly sensual Australian gal who is nobody’s idea of a delicate flower. Her chemistry with Pitt is off the charts. At one point Crosby, as Cliff calls her, is seen attending the splashy premiere of Looking for Mr. Goodbar , photographed like a goddess in a fabulously draped white halter pantsuit and scarf — an unwise choice later that evening when she goes to a mud-caked figure-eight track and is surprised to find Cliff among the drivers. Even in moments that might be considered humiliating for many screen glamazons, Karen’s authority never falters. And she is equally adept at delivering a left and right hook. Gugino also brings her A-game to a smart character who accepts her husband for the overgrown boy he is but by no means is immune to the flirty sexual frisson of a more mature hunk. The actress also looks nothing short of sensational. There’s not a weak link in the ensemble. Abdul-Mateen is very clearly having a blast playing outrageous stereotypes in the fictional film and TV scenes within the movie, and when Rod is not on a screen or in front of a camera he carries himself with the effortless swagger of a former pro-footballer turned badass movie star. The other vital cast contribution comes from Peter Weller as Cliff’s dad Gus, who, when not behind the counter at his pawn shop — where he teaches junkies how capitalism works — consumes an unending diet of TV, whether it’s The Rockford Files , Bonanza or Hee Haw . Father and son share an apartment in a sprawling Marina del Rey complex, where their spiky exchanges never obscure the nourishing love they get from each other. Mostly, Gus just wants Cliff to feed his cat and stop blocking the TV. While the ‘70s New Hollywood reference is clear, Fincher and cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt — shooting on digital, a departure from Tarantino’s devotion to celluloid — perhaps lean into the dark, grubby look a little too eagerly, though the noirish aspect fits, echoed in Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’ supple score. Courtesy of Ren Klyce’s densely layered sound design, those orchestral interludes are woven in with a dizzying array of needle drops that make you wonder how much Netflix spent on music rights. (The unexpected use of Electric Light Orchestra’s peppy “Tightrope” over one violent sequence is inspired, and there’s not one but two Donna Summer tracks that absolutely slap.) Production and costume design from Don Burt and Trish Summerville, respectively, are a riot of period nods that never drift into kitsch. Ultimately, however, the key ingredient binding together a movie that seldom meets an abrupt tangent it declines to explore is Pitt. His star wattage, shit-eating grin and cowboy gait — even with a limp and a body full of bones on which decades of stunt work have taken their toll — are dialed up to maximum magnetism. title: It Girl India Amarteifo’s Queen’s Gambit
full_text: × Skip to main content By Seija Rankin Plus Icon Seija Rankin Senior Editor seijawrites Follow Sign Up View All November 19, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source India Amarteifio was photographed at THR’s Cannes Portrait Studio. Photographed by Guy Aroch India Amarteifio went to bed on May 3, 2023, a working but largely unknown young actress. The next morning — after Netflix dropped Queen Charlotte : A Bridgerton Story , a prequel in which Amarteifio plays a younger version of Golda Rosheuvel’s imperious royal — she woke up famous. “The first thing I did that day was walk down the street with my co-star Corey [Mylchreest], and we were immediately recognized and stopped by fans,” she says. “We just looked at each other like, ‘OK, life has changed now.’ ” Three years later, Amarteifio, 25, is still getting stopped on the street — at least three or four times a day. “People still rewatch it, or a new Bridgerton comes out and puts the spotlight back on,” she says. “I do wonder whether I’m going to be Queen Charlotte forever.” Related Stories Movies A "Very Human" Father-Daughter Story: 'THR Presents' Q&A With Myrsini Aristidou on Cyprus' First Oscar Submission, 'Hold Onto Me' Movies The Free World Award Is Made From Weapons Metal. The First Winner: Iraq's Oscar Entry Not a bad problem to have, considering her previous career anxiety: that her days as an actor might already be finished. Amarteifio grew up in Southwest London, where acting classes helped burn off excess energy (“I was quite a bouncy child”). Her mother, a beautician, spotted newspaper advertisements for West End casting calls, leading to roles in The Lion King and Matilda , the latter an experience she likens to military training. She picked up representation and television work, including an episode of Sex Education , but graduated from drama school straight into the pandemic. “It’s so silly, but I wasn’t booking anything, and I thought, ‘My time has passed at 20 years old,’ ” she says with a laugh. Then came Queen Charlotte — and literal overnight success. The series instantly hit No. 1 on Netflix, topped Nielsen’s streaming charts and went on to surpass 80 million views, becoming one of the platform’s most popular titles. After waiting so long for her big break, Amarteifio was willing to wait a little longer for the right follow-up. She took a long pause after Queen Charlotte , thinking about the career she wanted beyond the show that had made her famous. The offers were coming, but she was holding out for “more art house, indie, character-driven” projects. She found what she was looking for in Clarissa , a Neon film from Nigerian twin filmmakers Arie and Chuko Esiri that opens in select U.S. theaters Dec. 11. Their reimagining of Mrs. Dalloway casts Hotel Rwanda Oscar nominee Sophie Okonedo as a Lagos society woman revisiting the summer that shaped her life, with Amarteifio taking over in the flashbacks. Ayo Edebiri and David Oyelowo round out the cast. Cast and crew lived communally at the Esiris’ family resort in Nigeria, canoeing to work daily. “You would look down at the turquoise of the water and look up to see monkeys jumping overhead, and it was unreal,” recalls Amarteifio. Amarteifio in Clarissa . Courtesy of Neon She also relished the chance to talk shop with her castmates. “I’m always just like, ‘Are you guys OK?’ ” she says with a laugh. “This industry can be so much sometimes, so I’m really interested in how people are doing and how they look after themselves. And, of course, I look at someone like Ayo and her trajectory and hope my career takes a similar form.” The film’s festival run, beginning at Cannes and taking her to Telluride, Toronto and New York, has brought her closer to the kind of attention she wants. “People care about the work, and they want to know about how it was created rather than the focus being on what you’re wearing or who you’re with,” Amarteifio notes. A movie musical remains on her wish list (“If you know of anyone who’s doing one!”), but otherwise she wants more of the same. Amarteifio’s fans, though, would prefer a busier release schedule. “Sometimes when I go on Instagram, I’ll see people saying, ‘Why isn’t she working? Why isn’t she on our screens?’ and I’m like, ‘Guys, do you not think things have been coming through my inbox?’ ” she says. “I have had opportunities, but I’m thinking smarter. I can’t be seen doing random nonsense because I need to think about the impact it will have for my trajectory.” This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: A “Very Human” Father-Daughter Story: ‘THR Presents’ Q&A With Myrsini Aristidou on Cyprus’ First Oscar Submission, ‘Hold Onto Me’

The film, starring newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis ( Dogtooth ), premiered at Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award. It follows Iris, 11, whose grandfather has died, which leads to petty criminal Aris — the father she has never known — arriving in town. Can what starts out as a stubborn attempt to connect develop into a fragile bond? Related Stories Movies The Free World Award Is Made From Weapons Metal. The First Winner: Iraq's Oscar Entry Movies "Hollywood Rewrites History" and Calls for Authentic Female Characters: Tallinn Debates Cinema Amid Global Crisis Hold Onto Me is a Cyprus-Denmark-Greece co-production that takes a deep dive into a beach community and is partially inspired by the filmmaker’s personal experience. During a taping of THR Presents , Aristidou shared how “the narrative arc of all my films is sort of a love story and the disappointments that come with it.” Hold Onto Me is based in Cyprus, but addresses universal themes. How would you describe what the film explores? And how important was it for you to show us characters who are not fully good or bad? The subject matter is something that I care about a lot — all of us [do], I think. Our relationship with our parents matters. It is something we carry with us. We either work on it to improve it or make it better or heal it — or many people let it go as well and just move on and try not to repeat the same patterns. … I care a lot about characters that are real, that are very imperfect, very human in their own way, and maybe even lonely in many ways. How did you cast young Maria as Iris? She had never done acting before, actually. Our casting director found her in Cyprus. She was younger than what I had written in the script. I wrote the script for a 15-year-old, and she was 10 and a half at the time. Yet, there was something about her. There was this innocence and authenticity. There is an emergency scene in the sea. I don’t imagine you had a big water tank that you filmed in? It was very, very different and complicated. We didn’t have the budget to shoot in a pool. We shot in the sea. It was very cold; we shot at night. … We were splashing water with our hands. Watch the full Q&A with Aristidou in the video above. THR

News of the new attempt at the Jane Hawk series comes as shows based on book characters with multiple novels to their name are more popular than ever. title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Review: Pitt, Fincher, And Tarantino Team Up For A Rollicking Good Wild Ride Of A ‘Hollywood’ Follow-Up
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Oscars: The 17th Governors Awards Highlight Long Overdue Recognition For Glenn Close, Ridley Scott, And More In A Warm And Heartfelt Evening Sony’s Tom Rothman Hopes It Will Be A ‘Brand New Day’ For ‘Spider-Man’ As Studio Launches Major Best Picture Oscar Campaign: “Are You Telling Me There Are 10 Films Better Than This One?” ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Blissfully Goes All Scrooge In Ti West’s New Horror-Flavored Take On Dickens Christmas Classic View All November 19, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth in 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' Netflix Whenever people ask me what my favorite movie of all time is I always have a hard time answering that impossible question, but if you want to know my favorite of the past ten years or so it’s simply. I can easily say Quentin Tarantino ‘s 2019 Once Upon A Time In Hollywood. So any idea of a sequel to this L.A. masterpiece set in 1969 that starred Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt as Rick Dalton, a movie star who has seen better days, and Cliff Booth his stunt man/sidekick has big shoes to fill following a movie that received 10 Oscar nominations and won 2 including Best Supporting Actor for Pitt. In my opinion it should also have won Best Picture and Director and Tarantino but I digress. Related Stories News Brad Pitt Backs Robert Pattinson As 007 & Jokingly Pitches Himself As Bond Villain: "I'd Like To Do That" Casting Brad Pitt To Star In 'Connector' From Apple And 'Sound Of Metal' Director Darius Marder Now with The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth we have one, or should I say “follow-up” since the filmmakers insist this is not a sequel but rather a continuation of the story of Booth set 8 years later in 1977 Hollywood, a bit of a darker time for Cliff and the town, at least in the world according to Q.T. Watch on Deadline This is the script Tarantino had written for a planned 10th and final directorial film but later scrapped for personal reasons. Pitt however didn’t want to let Cliff Booth go and enlisted David Fincher ,his director of Seven, Fight Club, and The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button to take it on, with Tarantino’s endorsement of course. Thus arguably the three most exciting filmmakers of their generation (they were all born within a year between 1962 and 1963) have teamed for a hell of an entertaining movie that delivers on every level an uber-fan of Once Upon A Time In Hollywood might expect – and then some – but these ‘mis-adventures’ are a whole new bag with a brand new set of characters surrounding Booth. Now it is the summer of ’77, a long time since Booth dispatched the members of the Manson clan in Tarantino’s parallel history of those real-life horrifying murders in his fairy tale of Hollywood circa ’69. Rick Dalton has moved on to Australia and a TV series. Booth is now working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema (the theatre Tarantino owns) and a part-time bartender at Lucy’s El Adobe restaurant across the street from Paramount in Hollywood. His other talents, displayed in disposing that tribe of hippies, as well as knocking out Bruce Lee, made him a bit of legendary lore in the town, a past he doesn’t really talk about much now but those talents will come in handy again. Just wait. Booth, still wearing those signature Hawaiian shirts, is a good son who often stops by to watch The Rockford Files and other TV shows with his elderly father, Gus ( Peter Weller ) who also runs a pawn shop and is a bit of a pistol himself. We know however from events at the theatre that start this follow-up that Cliff is also involved with some small time crime as the two thugs he employed to rob an Oscar winning director turn up with the loot and want their money. It’s complicated but Cliff is also a fixer who is capable of some pretty violent acts of his own. Say no more but it is an intriuging set up for what is to come. The main event arrives when he gets a call from a talent agent named Karen Crosby ( Elizabeth Debicki ) on behalf of her client, a big TV star named Charlie Peters ( Scott Caan ), but this is a guy known for doing his own stunts so why does he need Cliff? Nevertheless Cliff’s unique talents can serve as strong advice which he gives to Charlie whose own world is as shady as it comes and involves his wife Toni (Carla Gugino) who as it turns out had a romantic laiason with Cliff years earlier. There is also football great turned movie star Roderick ‘Hot Rod’ Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) , and most imposing, the terrifying Filipino Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), gangsters who are running around town causing violent chaos with a sledge hammer and some unfinished business for their own “clients” including Peters . Suffice to say all of these characters serve as a set up for a brusing crime story as familiar to Fincher fans as it might be to Tarantino’s. This tasty cinematic cocktail is explosive. If you wonder how this merger of Fincher and Tarantino will work, take comfort in the fact it is a shotgun marriage that fires on all cylinders, a dazzling display of directorial and writing talent unmatched in this genre that create a movie unlike any other out there, and that includes the remarkable one that birthed it. Pitt clearly knew this role was one he couldn’t easily let go of, even when Tarantino decided to deep six the script that would bring him back. Cliff Booth is such a mysterious, laid back guy, capable of anything but never showing his cards. The darker world we now find him inhabiting is startling but the essence of what he was once upon a time in another Hollywood is still there, just ramped up a bit to fit the changing times, and when the occasion arises he also knows how to dress for it. There is more in his closet, literally and figuritively, than those patented shirts. You can see why he won that supporting Oscar (and there is a very funny bit involving one of those during the opening scenes here), but now Pitt’s Booth has the starring role and he is a screen character for the ages. Surrounding him here is a sterling set of actors including the wonderful Debicki playing a woman whose own past is slowly revealed, and who also becomes, against all odds, a romantic interest for Booth in a relationship that is played out in a series of song dedications on local radio station KRLA, a pure Tarantino touch. Caan really gets a showcase here as the fast-talking TV star in a bit over his head. He is simply terrific, as is Weller who has never been better, a real re-discovery of an actor who inhabits the role of Booth’s dad with wise wit and warmth. The relationship here between father and son grounds the film in a very smart way, showing a human side of Cliff that balances the darker edges of this scenario perfectly. Props also to Gugino who is very fine balancing her rocky marriage to Charlie while also dealing with the emergence of her own past with Cliff. Abdul-Mateen II is ideal casting as a Jim Brown type who will figure into all this mayhem. In fact we first meet him right at the start in a Tarantino specialty, a scene with an unbilled Samuel L. Jackson that turns out to be the blackploitation movie Cliff is running at this theatre. Timothy Olyphant also has a delicious cameo as actor James Stacy. And then there are the Verducso brothers played to the evil hilt by Groove and Tadena who both make about as gruesome a pair you will ever encounter. Welcome to hard times. The script is full of easter eggs and wry movie and tv references, a pop culture bible of the time that only Tarantino and his brilliant wordsmithing could cook up, and though I am loathe to say he tops himself here, I will say this screenplay matches our expectations in every way. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth is vintage Tarantino and we are indebted to Fincher for delivering it in style. The director sharply shows off his own unique talents in a movie that never slows down, even with the signature QT monologues, or the fantastic Tarantino-narrated documentary on the career of Charlie Peters. There is so much here this movie will require more than one viewing, that’s for sure. Production wise it is all top of the game across the board including many who have worked with Fincher numerous times including Kirk Baxter’s complex editing, Erik Messerschmidt’s stunning cinematography, Ren Klyce’s complex sound design, Trish Summerville’s right-on 70’s costume design, and the pitch perfect production design of Donald Graham Burt. The score from Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross also hits the bullseye blending with the songs roaring through the ace soundtrack. And shout out to all the real stunt men employed. The finale is a real corker. Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt have hit another one straight out of the park. Producers are Ceán Chaffin and Pitt. title: Indie Distribution Exec Kyle Greenberg Exiting Utopia To Launch New Consultancy, Greenhouse
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill David Ellison Goes Personal: Raised By Single Mom, Bonded With Dad As Teen, Massive VHS Collection Sam Altman On ‘Artificial’ Movie About Him — Not Among “Ten Weirdest Things In My Life” Right Now David Ellison Commits To Airing Alex Gibney ‘Musk’ Doc On HBO Max, Calls Skydance Investor “Greatest Entrepreneur Of Our Time” View All November 19, 2026 9:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kyle Greenberg Sam Coyle EXCLUSIVE : Kyle Greenberg , longtime head of marketing and distribution at Utopia , is departing the company to launch a consulting startup called Greenhouse . His new venture plans to develop highly curated, hands-on release strategies for filmmakers, artists, labels and brands to support their own efforts in self-distribution, something an increasing number of producers are turning to given challenges in the current indie film landscape. Utopia was co-founded by Robert Schwartzman and Cole Harper in 2018. Greenberg helped launch the indie distribution, production and sales company, and its service-based Circle Collective division and has been a key player in growing both, overseeing creative, publicity and marketing, theatrical, home video, physical media and streaming for over 100 films. Related Stories News Utopia's Circle Collective Takes North American To 'Honeyjoon' Acquisitions Utopia's Circle Collective Acquires Greg Vrotsos' Silver Lake-Set 'Situations' He championed breakout and award-winning features from first-time and auteur filmmakers like Emma Seligman ( Shiva Baby ), Jane Schoenbrun ( We’re All Going To The World’s Fair ), Kristoffer Borgli ( Sick Of Myself ), Sean Price Williams ( The Sweet East ), Amalia Ulman ( El Planeta ), Alex Ross Perry ( Pavements ), Gaspar Noe ( Vortex ), Anton Corbijn ( Squaring The Circle, The Story of Hipgnosis ), Errol Morris ( American Dharma ), Ali Abbasi ( Holy Spider ), the Ross Brothers ( Bloody Nose, Empty Pockets ) and others. He worked with Francis Ford Coppola to market and book Megalopolis , and with Mike Figgis on Megadoc . Watch on Deadline His rollouts often merged non-traditional marketing and distribution, including bringing films to non-theatrical spaces with expansive elements like DJ sets, musical performances, art shows, pool parties and movie-date meetups, with a traditional, platformed theatrical or event strategy to build a footprint for independent and arthouse feature films across the U.S., U.K. and Canada. “While so many people in the industry are lamenting a lack of reliable distribution methods, Greenhouse will be an extension of the ethos that has served as the foundation of my career — growth through disruption,” he said. Greenberg is based in LA. He’ll be with Utopia through year end. He also plans to scale up his own production label Stupid Co, created in 2024, alongside Greenhouse. Founded as a showcase for original work produced by Greenberg and partner Anna Maguire, Stupid Co expanded to events and experiences Cannes Dogs, Off-Viff and info labs Stupid Chats. It will release Greenberg and Maguire’s co-directed feature Galicia! in 2027. The hybrid documentary-eco horror comedy, shot on location at a winery in Spain, premiered at The Downtown Festival in NYC last month. The couple’s short films Hi! title: A Pop-Star Acting Newbie, the Afterlife and “Dirty Energy”: The Making of ‘La Bola Negra’
full_text: × Skip to main content Milo Quifes films one of the movie’s final scenes in the Sierra Nevada mountain range. Carla Oset/Netflix Javier Calvo was traveling with his filmmaking partner, Javier Ambrossi, when he read Alberto Conejero’s play La Piedra Oscura ( The Dark Stone ) and the idea for La Bola Negra ( The Black Ball ) took hold. Conejero’s drama, set in a military hospital during the Spanish Civil War, imagines the last night of Rafael Rodríguez Rapún — a Republican lieutenant and the real-life lover of playwright Federico García Lorca — in conversation with Sebastián, the young Nationalist soldier who is to execute him at dawn. “I imagined this little gay boy having to leave his town, all this tragedy, and how this happened to my country only 90 years ago, and having a gay character in the civil war,” says Calvo. “We never talk about that. Where were we? What happened to us? It hit me, and I started to cry. I told Javi, ‘I think we have to make this.’ ” Related Stories Movies 'Obsession' Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Spotlight Tribute at Gotham Film Awards (Exclusive) Movies The Free World Award Is Made From Weapons Metal. The First Winner: Iraq's Oscar Entry The film, co-written with Conejero, braids three timelines. In 1932 Granada, Carlos (Milo Quifes), a young upper-class Andalusian, is blackballed from an exclusive casino because he’s gay — the premise of Lorca’s unfinished play La Bola Negra , of which only four pages survive. In 1937, Sebastián (singer- songwriter Guitarricadelafuente ) keeps watch over Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau). And in 2017 Madrid, Alberto (Carlos González) learns that he is Sebastián’s grandson. Sebastián has left him the rest of Lorca’s play — pages the film imagines into being — which he had promised Rafael he would save. Those pages — verified by Glenn Close, who plays a Spanish-speaking American scholar named Isabelle Durand — lead Alberto and his relatives to discover that Sebastián spent most of his life secretly living with another man. The casino from which Carlos (Milo Quifes) is banned was the only structure that was built for the film. Carla Oset/Netflix “This is a movie about what we pass on to the next generation,” Ambrossi says. “It’s about inheritance.” The co-directors, known as Los Javis among their collaborators because of their shared first names, reassembled their usual crafts team to begin shaping each timeline: cinematographer Gris Jordana, editor Alberto Gutiérrez, production designer Roger Bellés, costume designer Ana López Cobos, composer Raül Refree and casting directors Eva Leira and Yolanda Serrano. Javier Ambrossi outside of a 1937 seminary that was turned into an army hospital. Carla Oset/Netflix The directors were already keen on Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau for their respective roles, as well as González for the part of Alberto, which Ambrossi calls “a creation.” “He’s so comedic and flamboyant, but we wanted to give him a role where he can prove the actor that he is because sometimes queer people are given the same [stereotypical] roles,” Ambrossi says. Quifes, who like Guitarricadelafuente makes his screen debut in the film, was found through an open casting call. “He has a sense of melancholy about him, but it’s not about hopelessness; there’s a sense of hope and beauty,” says Leira. “And he has such a beautiful gaze. It’s a gaze that comes from ancient times.” Los Javis also knew they wanted to shoot in 35mm from the outset, which aligned with DP Jordana’s approach. “You don’t have to fight the format to get images,” she says of 35mm film. “If you use the right light direction, the rest just comes together. It’s like magic.” Light also drove the design of the opulent casino in Granada, the only set built from scratch. Everywhere else, the production restored existing buildings, hiring local artisans who still work with prewar methods. “At first glance, it looked like something crazy and unnecessary when we built it in the middle of Spain, but when you open the windows, you see Spain, not a green screen,” says production designer Bellés, who commissioned artist Ignasi Monreal to paint the mural on the ceiling in the style of Joaquín Sorolla, “one of the great painters of Spanish light,” he explains. The windows were made of sugar glass so that they could shatter safely when the casino explodes near the end of the film after being overtaken by a mob as Carlos makes a final case for admission. The remaining structure was then filled with fake snow as the scene transitions to Carlos lying on a mountainside, realizing he has died from the bomb’s explosion. The shot, captured at an altitude of 3,000 meters (more than 9,800 feet high) in the snowy region of the Sierra Nevadas, brought to life elements described in Lorca’s poem — like the skiers on the slopes — which also inspired Guitarricadelafuente’s original song, “La Nieve (The Snow),” that plays in the background. “With Federico García Lorca, there’s a lot of powerful imagery and symbolism, like in the beginning of the film, the horse running past Sebastián is a representation of untamable desire,” Guitarricadelafuente explains. “ ‘La Nieve’ symbolized the end of a journey and approaching death. I had to leave the emotional baggage of Sebastián to fully understand what he was carrying to be able to write that.” Penélope Cruz portrays a cupletista cabaret singer named Nené Romero in a La Bola Negra. Carla Oset/Netflix Refree took a hands-on approach with Penélope Cruz, who portrays Nené Romero, a cupletista cabaret singer. “She told me, ‘I’m not a singer,’ but as soon as I heard her singing … I fell in love with her singing,” he says. “The problem was that she hadn’t created the character yet.” Over the course of several days, Refree went to Cruz’s home for rehearsals, and she began to craft the persona of Nené, who serves as a portal to a world in which Sebastián can be free to be his true self when he sees her perform “Las Tardes del Ritz (Afternoons at the Ritz)” and “Batallón de modistillas (Seamstress Battalion)” on the base. “My goal was to have this kind of music that she could be influenced by when talking to the soldiers and to create this evocative thing, like making two men play together as a couple,” Refree explains of the first number. “The second one needed a dirty energy that would make the soldiers lose control and want to touch her. So we created something very rhythmic and feminine at the same time.” Wardrobe also helped shape Nené. Cobos drew from research on 19th century cuplé singers, like María del Consuelo Vello Cano, to sketch Cruz’s feathery, embellished ensemble. The abandoned village of Castil de Carrias in the province of Burgos, Spain, was restored for the opening scene in which an Italian aircraft bombs civilians. Carla Oset/Netflix “When she saw the white dress, she said, ‘This is it; she has to be wearing white,’ and Gris also said it would be helpful because we don’t have a lot of lights in the theater,” says Cobos. “[For the second number,] because I know Penélope’s a big fan of Mugler, I went through their images and found these overalls and dresses that reminded me of military costumes. So I did my own interpretation of them, and it worked really well because it helped her move and it was very comfortable for her to do the choreography with the tank and all of the other dancers.” In the final scene of the film, Sebastián reads a poem with the words, “ Mira, que nos acechan todavia (Beware, they still haunt us),” after being forced to shoot Rafael. It’s the final verse of “Love Sleeps in the Poet’s Breast,” one of the Sonetos del Amor Oscuro ( Sonnets of Dark Love ), written by Lorca for Rafael, expressing his forbidden desire for him amid the looming threat of societal persecution. For Calvo, the warning is just as relevant today. “We had it on the whiteboard, and it was kind of a guide [for us],” he says. “Putting it [at the end of the film] was perfect and so significant because they do still haunt us.” Miguel Bernardeau (left) portrays poet Federico García Lorca’s real-life lover Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, and Guitarricadelafuente stars as Sebastián. Carla Oset/Netflix This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Stephen Colbert Signs With UTA
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All November 19, 2026 9:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Stephen Colbert Mary Ellen Matthews/CBS Stephen Colbert has signed with UTA as he explores opportunities after The Late Show concluded earlier this year, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. UTA will be representing the 13-time Emmy winner as well as his production company, Spartina Industries, across film, television, publishing work and more. “We are thrilled to be working with Stephen Colbert. He is an exceptionally talented artist and creator, a dedicated philanthropist and a terrific person,” UTA president of filmed entertainment Matt Rice and managing partners Jay Gassner and Julien Thuan said in a joint statement. “We look forward to partnering with Stephen and Spartina Industries to support and further expand his creative endeavors.” Colbert signed off from The Late Show in May after hosting the late-night series, which became a casualty of the Paramount-Skydance merger , for a decade. In the process, the comedian — who also wrote on and executive produced the series — collected several of his many Emmys as well as a Peabody Award. Prior to his tenure at The Late Show , Colbert hosted, wrote and produced Comedy Central’s satire news program The Colbert Report for nine years and wrote and served as a correspondent on The Daily Show for seven years. And Colbert is keeping busy post- Late Show . Currently, he’s co-writing the next Lord of the Rings movie with veteran LOTR screenwriter Philippa Boyens and his son Peter McGee, as well as working on his screenwriting software company Scripto. In a recent interview with THR , Colbert said he has been entertaining other opportunities but hasn’t landed on one yet. “There’s some fun stuff to think about. I’m in no hurry,” he said. His production company, Spartina Industries, is currently developing a TV adaptation of Roger Zelazny’s sci-fi book series The Chronicles of Amber with The Walking Dead co-creator Robert Kirkman’s Skybound Entertainment. The company, headed up by Carrie Byalick, previously produced two seasons of the late-night show After Midnight on CBS. Colbert continues to be managed by James Baby Doll Dixon at Dixon Talent, Inc. and represented by Tom Hansen and Don Steele at Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman. THR

title: ‘Aurora’ Short Film Team Angad Aulakh And Guy Kent On Tapping Into The Emotional Weight Of Self & Outer Space
full_text: Skip to main content By Destiny Jackson Destiny Jackson Crafts Editor, Awards @DestinyDreadful More Stories By Destiny ‘Primetime’ Cinematographer & Editor On Making Robert Pattinson Look Like A “Superhero” & Breakdown Viral Meme Catchphrase ‘Being Heumann’ Star Ruth Madeley And Casting Team On Championing Diversity Onscreen – Contenders L.A. ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Star Mahershala Ali Says It Can Be “Dangerous That People End Up Believing Their Own Righteousness” — Contenders L.A. View All November 19, 2026 9:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Guy Kent in 'Aurora'. Angad Aulakh ’s lifelong fascination with space inspired Aurora, a sci-fi short about an astronaut left stranded after a mission goes catastrophically wrong. Freddie Ballard ( Guy Kent ) is sent to investigate a mysterious signal, but an accident makes him the sole survivor, with no way home and growing doubts about what his superiors have told him. Shot in black and white, the film draws on German Expressionism and retro-futurism to create its unique visual world. Aulakh and Kent talk to Deadline about shaping Freddie’s journey, building the film’s cosmic scale on a short-film budget and their plans for what lies beyond the vast reaches of the galaxy they created. Related Stories News Actor Russell Tovey Dismantles The Manosphere In His Award-Winning Performance In 'I Am The Prize' News 'Vultures' Swoops To Top Award At Oscar-Qualifying HollyShorts Film Festival: Winners List DEADLINE: How did you come up with this concept? Watch on Deadline ANGAD AULAKH: It really started with a lifelong obsession with space and the idea that we are not alone in the universe. It’s one of the most compelling ideas for storytellers and people in general. When we look at how short our lives are, how small Earth is and how vast the universe is, the possibilities for what’s out there are so exciting. It’s the idea that we might not even be asking the right questions yet. We don’t know which questions to ask because there are concepts so grand and profound. Exploring them through storytelling felt like a wonderful opportunity. With short films, you have more leeway to be a little avant-garde. I often liken short films to haikus, while features are full-fledged novels. So I wanted to focus on the emotion, the moment, the visuals and the wonder of space. Technology has evolved so much that it’s why we can make a film like this on our budget today. I’m happy to say we didn’t use any AI on the film. I’m not throwing shade at AI, by any means, but I know it’s a big part of the conversation right now. It started with looking up at the stars and wondering what’s out there and what stories I could explore in the vastness of space. Aurora Last Carnival DEADLINE: Guy, I read that the two of you have partnered on several projects. Is this one the most ethereal? When you heard about the idea, what went through your mind? GUY KENT: I was thrilled because I also have a lifelong fascination with space and our place in [the cosmos]. As Angad said, we have so many questions and no answers. Finding some faith that there’s meaning despite not having the answers is profound to me. When this idea came up, it was an exciting adventure to embark on. Angad and I have been deliberate about budget and scope, especially with short films. We prioritize quality and want to understand what we can and can’t achieve. With this film, the next question was, “How are we going to pull this off? How do we make it feel like the work we want to do, while making sure it works, resonates and lets the emotional moments land?” Our pre-production work and the team we’ve worked with in the past gave us a built-in shorthand. That was especially true with our cinematographer, but finding a stage where we could create a set and build on it was also a huge part of making this feasible. DEADLINE: The short film rests on you, Guy. You have a lot of scenes on your own. Your character is not only lost in space, but lost to himself, or somewhere in between. How did the two of you work on that story? What would you like audiences to think about through that juxtaposition? KENT: Angad and I had a lot of discussions that began with isolation. Isolation isn’t something you show; it’s something you sit in. It’s revealing to see what happens when all distractions are removed and there’s no barrier between you and your own thoughts. For Freddie, there’s a chance to find himself again. He’s an astronaut trained for crisis, someone who understands how to solve most of the problems he faces. Here, he’s confronted with something very personal and existential that he has no answers for. It would be interesting if audiences were left wondering not only how they would react to meeting something beyond Earth, but also considering the hope that there’s something greater. As Angad said, even if we don’t have answers to these questions, there can be meaning in an unknowable answer. That makes you feel found in a way. DEADLINE: Angad, what was the hardest thing about putting this story together? AULAKH: The biggest challenge was looking at short films as a whole and thinking about how much time we had and how long the film would be. There are practical considerations, too. A lot of festivals won’t accept a short film longer than 15 minutes. AULAKH: There are practical considerations around the film’s life after it’s released, but audiences also expect a short film to be short. Ideally, you’re not making a 30- or 40-minute short, because then you might as well make a feature. We had to think about the real estate available to us and the most effective way to make audiences leave having felt something and gone on an emotional experience. That’s what I’m interested in as a filmmaker: moving people. A big part of that is considering how the music, sound design, performance and production design work together to convey something cinematic and effective. You also want to tell a compelling story. Weaving Freddie’s journey into a cohesive narrative in 15 minutes was always going to be a challenge, but I’m pleased with how it turned out. We focused on the emotion and on the fact that a mission has gone wrong. This astronaut is either going to be killed aboard the spacecraft or find his way home. I hoped the quieter moments would sustain the audience because they’d want to stick around to see whether Freddie makes it. DEADLINE: Let’s talk about the scope of the film. The cinematography is great. Why black and white as your color scheme? AULAKH: German Expressionism was on my mind as I wrote the screenplay and thought about the aesthetic I wanted. The other reason is that we don’t see many black-and-white films set in space or black-and-white science-fiction films. More than anything, I think it looks gorgeous on screen. The light on the set, shining through the top grates, was beautiful. We had scouted locations beforehand, so we knew what the set would look like. But the first image that came to mind was Freddie Ballard lying on the floor, screaming and tumbling. I saw it in black and white. I hadn’t shot a black-and-white film since film school, and I thought this was the perfect opportunity. The stars look beautiful in black and white. There was also a practical reason. Black and white is more forgiving when you don’t have a huge budget for production design. You can hide things in the shadows, and it worked well with our special effects and the 3D modeling. We also made sequences in Unreal Engine with Stuart Lippincott, who’s an absolute genius. His work was a huge inspiration to me. I thought the lighting, images, and compositions would be tremendous in black and white. KENT: On an emotional level, I think black and white subconsciously creates a sense of melancholy. That’s the basis of German Expressionism, at least in my experience. There’s an emotional texture it brings. AULAKH: Yeah, it’s very melancholic. Black and white also has inherent cinematic associations. Audiences think of films from the 1930s and ’40s, most of which were made in black and white. I love the idea that Aurora can feel like a product of the past, something you might have seen in those bygone eras. That was exciting because retro-futurism, which is used extensively in science-fiction films and video games, is powerful and interesting. I gravitate toward it, so I loved being able to use that aesthetic in Aurora . Aurora Last Carnival DEADLINE: What were the biggest technical challenges, and where did you have to get especially inventive? You’ve talked about using black and white, but is there another example? How did you get inventive with the production design? AULAKH: A lot of the credit goes to our visual effects artist, Ian Mills Miller. The entity you see in the film was originally going to be an actor, Ethan [Daniel Corbett], wearing a latex bodysuit. We were going to use his movements and digitally map them onto a being, the way they did with Gollum in The Lord of the Rings . Instead, we used Ethan as a reference, and Ian created the magnificent 3D being you see in the film. That’s a hard shot to pull off because it’s expensive and time-consuming, and you have to be careful about how much you show. Black and white allowed us to hide the entity in the shadows. He’s a being of light at the end of the film, but throughout it he looks dark and mechanical. He’s influenced more by machinery than by alien life. It was tricky. Having the ability to hide him in the shadows and take a less-is-more approach was effective. If you hold an effects shot too long, the audience may start to look at it differently. Even in major motion pictures, it can be disconcerting and create an uncanny valley effect. We wanted to avoid that with our digital effects. DEADLINE: Talk a bit about your experience on the film festival circuit. AULAKH: I’ll take the first part, and Guy can talk about where we’ve been and what’s coming up. We premiered at HollyShorts this August, which was a lovely experience. I’m a small-town kid from Mountaintop, Pennsylvania. We didn’t have a movie theater in town, and we still don’t. Getting to screen a film at the historic Grauman’s Chinese Theatre was an honor. The festival was so well put together, and the audience response was wonderful. There were events throughout the week, so you had a chance to meet other filmmakers and talk with people watching your film. As a filmmaker, you get real-time feedback from the room. Unfortunately, we can’t attend many festivals because they’re all over the world. The few opportunities we get to sit with an audience and see the film on the big screen are phenomenal. It’s been wonderful so far. Our last few shorts had great festival runs, and we hope Aurora will top both of them. We’re just getting started. Guy can tell you more about where we’re headed next. KENT: We’re going to FilmQuest. We are nominated for Best Sci-Fi Short and Best Visual Effects, which is fantastic. We’re thrilled to be part of that festival and what it represents. They’ve been wonderful. We’ve also done Anomaly Film Festival and Toronto Arthouse, and we’re going to Festival of Fantastic Films in the U.K. We have some other festivals to be announced toward the end of the year and early next year. The greatest thing, as Angad said, is connecting with audiences and getting the film’s message out there. I think it’s a special piece, and there’s more to this world that we hope to build beyond the short. The more audiences see it, the more we’ll be able to go down that road. AULAKH: We’re developing a television series based on Aurora and its world. If we can build some excitement throughout the festival circuit, it’ll make getting the series off the ground that much easier. We hope people respond to the film. After the festival circuit, we’ll release it online; we’re working on distribution for that, too. These festival runs can last upwards of a year and a half, if you’re lucky. We’re excited to get the film out there around the world, and it has officially gone international. Sometimes things can go right in life, and this is luckily one of those situations. I don’t want to knock on wood as I say that. We’re thrilled and honored to be selected. title: ‘Birthright,’ About Differing Attitudes on Israel, Set For Broadway
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All November 19, 2026 9:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Off-Broadway cast of 'Birthright.' Emilio Madrid Birthright, a play by Tony Award winner Jonathan Spector examining differing views about Israel among Jewish-American friends, will move to Broadway this spring. The play is set for a 20-week run at Broadway’s Hudson Theatre starting Feb. 23, 2027, ahead of a March 15 opening night. It moves to Broadway after a sold-out and critically acclaimed run at the Off-Broadway MCC Theater this past summer. Teddy Bergman directs, making his Broadway debut after helming the Off-Broadway run. Casting for the Broadway run has not yet been announced. The play follows seven friends through 18 years, starting just after their Birthright trip to Israel in 2006, tracking their differing and changing attitudes on Israel as well as changes within their own lives. Spector returns to Broadway after last season’s Eureka Day, which won the Tony Award for best revival of a play, and centered on a school board dealing with select parents who did not want to vaccinate their kids. “Just over two years ago, I was racing to finish a first draft of Birthright before starting rehearsals for Eureka Day at MTC. I could never have fathomed that such a short time later we’d be bringing it to Broadway, when the questions the play is wrestling with still feel so close to our present moment. Writing this was the scariest thing I’ve ever attempted to do, and (perhaps not coincidentally), has become the most meaningful and rewarding. I’m beyond thrilled that a wider audience will have a chance to encounter the play and see the work of our brilliant artistic collaborators,” Spector said. THR

Terms of the agreement were not disclosed, but Imax has signed its first deal with Showcase Cinemas, and also with a longtime business partner. “I’ve been in the Imax business for decades and the value of its technology, brand, and strategic partnership to exhibitors have grown exponentially in that time,” Greidinger said in a statement after his recent acquisition of the 16-venue Showcase Cinemas circuit from Skydance. “There is no doubt that Imax plays a significant role in the results of the industry and I am sure it will continue to grow and attract new audience and become even more significant in the coming years. The new laser projection systems will go in 12 U.K. locations and another in Europe. Regal owner Cineworld in 2023 emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceeding in the U.S. via a restructuring, with Greidinger and his management team eventually leaving the British cinema operator. “Mooky is a visionary leader and an excellent partner who recognized the value in Imax long before our recent run of record-breaking success. title: ‘My Favorite Murder’ HBO Series Sets December Premiere
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All November 19, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Karen Kilgariff and Georgia Hardstark HBO There are so many platforms where one can stay sexy and not get murdered these days. HBO is the latest to get in business with Karen Kilgariff and Georgia Hardstark ‘s My Favorite Murder , turning their hit true crime comedy podcast into a docuseries. Also called My Favorite Murder , the four-part project chronicles the pair’s 2025 sold-out American tour. It follows the format of their long-running podcast — the women trade grim stories with a respectful dose of levity — while also turning an eye to the devoted community of listers (aka “Murderinos”) who have followed the pair for over a decade. “The question everyone asks us is always, ‘Why do women love true crime so much?'” Kilgariff told The Hollywood Reporter earlier this year . “So we’re letting them tell you. We can’t ever answer that correctly. Other people have answers, but they’re all personal, so let’s get them.” Related Stories TV Melissa Gorga to Debut 'Sunday Sauce' Video Podcast This December (Exclusive) Business How 'The Basement Yard' Host Joe Santagato Got Into the World of 'Hot Ones' Premiering Dec. 3, the series airs on Thursdays through the rest of 2026 — with episodes recorded during Chicago, Pasadena, Boston and Brooklyn shows. It is executive produced by Kilgariff and Hardstark, as well as showrunner, Page Hurwitz. The series comes from Liz Garbus and Dan Cogan’s Story Syndicate as well as HBO Documentary Films . Turning 10 years old in January, this is not My Favorite Murder ‘s first pivot to TV. Kilgariff and Hardstark’s Exactly Right Media signed a pact with Netflix last December to bring a video version of the podcast to the streamer where it now airs weekly. HBO released these summaries of its My Favorite Murder series, which will naturally stream on HBO Max as well. Episode 1: Chicago Debut date: Thursday, Dec. 3 (9:00-9:59 p.m. ET/PT) At The Chicago Theater, Karen and Georgia dig into the shocking hate crime murders of a prominent mid-western hairstylist and a noted cosmetic surgeon and then tell the fascinating tale of Alice Clement – the first female detective in the Prohibition-era city. Episode 2: Pasadena Debut date: Thursday, Dec. 10 (9:00-9:58 p.m. ET/PT) At The Pasadena Civic Auditorium, in their hometown of the wider Los Angeles area, the podcasters look into the case of the “80s sex, drugs, and ‘Just Sweats’ insurance scandal,” as well as the bizarre, botched kidnapping of Frank Sinatra Jr. Episode 3: Boston Debut date: Thursday, Dec. 17 (9:00-9:59 p.m. ET/PT) At The Boch Center Wang Theatre, Karen and Georgia dissect the still unsolved disappearance of wife and mother Joan Risch in 1961, which some see as the inspiration for the film Gone Girl, as well as the famed 1978 blizzard that ground the city to a halt and led to some unexpected “sleepovers.” Episode 4: Brooklyn Debut date: Thursday, Dec. 24 (9:00-10:00 p.m. ET/PT) At the Kings Theatre, the hosts take a deeper look at the infamous Scarsdale diet doctor murder, and then follow the peculiar case of the red bees of Red Hook, Brooklyn that led to a shocking discovery in the basement of a nearby maraschino cherry warehouse.
