title: AI Filmmaking Gets Its Awards Season: The Chroma Awards Return for a Bigger Second Year
full_text: × Nov 19, 2026 9:00am PT Partner Content AI Filmmaking Gets Its Awards Season: The Chroma Awards Return for a Bigger Second Year Submissions are open to creators worldwide through Jan. 7, 2027 By Partner Content Plus Icon Partner Content Latest China Film Pavilion Marks Its Fourth Consecutive Year at AFM 6 days ago Media City Qatar Supports Regional Productions All the Way to the Big Screen 1 week ago The Production Studio, Reimagined 3 weeks ago See All When the Chroma Awards opened for entries for the first time in 2025, its organizers bet that a global community of AI-native creators was ready for a stage of its own. More than 6,600 submissions poured in from 5,550 creators across 122 countries, spanning film, music videos, advertising and video games. Now, that stage is getting bigger. ElevenLabs , in partnership with CapCut , Cantina and Runware , has launched the second season of the Chroma Awards, with submissions open to creators worldwide through Jan. 7, 2027. Winners will be revealed during a global livestream in mid-February and later celebrated at an inaugural red-carpet awards gala. Related Stories Queen Latifah, Bone Thugs-N-Harmony, MC Lyte and More to Lead 2027 Rock the Bells Cruise “We’re incredibly grateful to our partners for their support in bringing this competition to life, supporting artists with over $1M in promotional giveaways and $450,000 in cash prizes and travel perks,” said Matty Shimura at the Chroma Awards. First founded in 2024 by ElevenLabs, the Chroma Awards has grown into a rallying point for the technology and creative communities alike. Industry partners, including Kling AI, OpenArt, Meshy, Floyo, Dreamina, Creatify, Magnific, Alibaba Cloud, Hyper3D, fal, A16Z, Cars24, ReelShort, Ashurst Perkins Coie, Fairground, Escape and Variety, partner in the competition to provide real opportunities for entrants. Beyond the prize pool, the competition provides free software trials, educational resources and direct industry exposure in a deliberate effort to lower the barriers that have historically kept emerging filmmakers on the outside looking in. “With the Chroma Awards, we want to bring emerging technology and creative talent into the same conversation and give creators across film, music, games and advertising a path to opportunities with the companies shaping these industries,” said Ameri Amin, Product and Growth at ElevenLabs. A New Spotlight on Process Season 2 keeps the divisions that defined the competition’s debut — film, music videos, advertising and video games — while adding something new: a dedicated behind-the-scenes division that emphasizes the creative process behind AI film production. “Some of the most original work happening right now is coming from people who never had a path to film, music or games before,” said Darren Lachtman, chief partnership officer at Cantina. “Those ideas deserve an audience, and the creator behind them deserves the tools and opportunities to keep building.” The addition reflects a growing conviction among the competition’s organizers that the story of AI filmmaking is not just about the finished work but about the people and craft behind it. “We are proud to offer creators the tools to take their ideas from concept to reality. This year, we want to highlight the artists behind the scenes whose creativity, humanity and craftsmanship make these projects possible,” said Ana Kley, head of U.S. Creator Operations at CapCut. Judged on Craft — and Integrity NEW YORK, NEW YORK – NOVEMBER 11: (L-R) Matty Shimura, Lead Organizer, Chroma Awards; Darren Lachtman, Chief Partnerships Officer, Cantina Labs; Carlos Roman, Head of Revenue, Runware and Aneri Amin, Product and Growth, llElevenLabs pose for a photo during ElevenLabs New York Summit at Lincoln Center on November 11, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Cindy Ord/Getty Images for ElevenLabs) Getty Images for ElevenLabs Entries will be evaluated by a diverse global panel of judges whose professional backgrounds span both traditional entertainment and the AI industry, ensuring that work is measured by cinematic standards as well as fluency with emerging tools. All submissions must also adhere to strict judging criteria regarding copyright, intellectual property and likeness rights, part of the Chroma Awards’ commitment to artistic integrity and a signal to the wider industry that AI-assisted creativity and rights protection can go hand in hand. “The cost of running AI at scale is still the biggest barrier between a good idea and a finished product,” said Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder at Runware. “By supporting the Chroma Awards, we are changing the economics of AI to support creators, brands and companies by putting that access back into the hands of the people building what comes next.” For the thousands of creators expected to answer this season’s call, that mission now comes with a deadline. Submissions for Season 2 of the Chroma Awards are open through Jan. 7, 2027, at http://submit.chromaawards.com/go/variety . title: John Muszynski, Who Spent Decades Carefully Deciding Whether Disney, Fox, Even Netflix, Would Get Millions in Ad Dollars, Plans to Retire
full_text: × Nov 19, 2026 9:00am PT John Muszynski, Who Spent Decades Carefully Deciding Whether Disney, Fox, Even Netflix, Would Get Millions in Ad Dollars, Plans to Retire By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest John Muszynski, Who Spent Decades Carefully Deciding Whether Disney, Fox, Even Netflix, Would Get Millions in Ad Dollars, Plans to Retire 1 hour ago ESPN Taps John Legend to Warm Up Crowds for CFP With Original Music 3 hours ago Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter Media Brings HBCU Basketball to BET 3 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Publicis Media John Muszynski never worked for the company known at various times as Time Warner, AOL Time Warner, WarnerMedia or Warner Bros. Discovery. He did, however, have a hand in at least one part of its operations. About 25 years ago, when “cable” represented a rapidly growing line of business and “streaming” had something to do with water, Muszynski was on a hunting trip outside of Atlanta with Mark Lazarus, at the time a senior executive at Warner’s TV operations. Lazarus says the pair were hunting for quail. Muszynski, one of the industry’s most senior — and most seasoned — media buyers , says the duo was chasing pheasant. No matter what the game was, the two executives devised what would eventually become a much greater prize. Related Stories Queen Latifah, Bone Thugs-N-Harmony, MC Lyte and More to Lead 2027 Rock the Bells Cruise “What I remember asking is, ‘What can we do as a company that would make you want to spend more money with us?’” recalls Lazarus, now the CEO of Versant, the owner of MS NOW, CNBC and other media properties. “He said, ‘I need something to compete with MTV. Right now, they are the only place that has the young people.’ We had Adult Swim at the time, but it was only on three hours a week. ‘It’s not enough to move money, not enough leverage for me with the Viacom folks,’” Muszynski told him. “I went back to the group that did content, and said, ‘We have to try to expand Adult Swim,’” Lazarus remembers. Over time, the gambit proved fruitful. Adult Swim, once a small piece of the schedule on Warner’s Cartoon Network, became a regular nighttime offering and captured the attention of a very difficult audience to reach — young men. “He was absolutely a catalyst, and opened our eyes,” says Lazarus. “He gave us a reason to really take a bigger risk.” Someone else will have to offer such suggestions in the future. Muszysnki, the U.S. chairman of Publicis Media Exchange, is stepping away from the role. And while he will serve as a consultant to the company in 2027, his departure will mark the end of an era, of sorts, as media becomes much more reliant on technology that seems to be moving many of its best-known outlets closer to obsolescence. Over nearly half a century, Muszynski worked for French ad giant Publicis Groupe, and before that the legendary U.S. advertising company Leo Burnett. His job? Placing billions of ad dollars across the U.S. media sector on behalf of clients that have encompassed blue-chip spenders ranging from the U.S. Army to McDonald’s, Kellogg’s and Molson Coors. He never ran a movie studio, a TV-news division or a sports operation. He never put together a must-see primetime TV schedule or devised a streaming-video hit. If anyone ever gave out an award for “Most Influential Media Executive the Average Person Has Never Heard Of,” Muszysnki would be a candidate to win. “As the industry evolved, John not only evolved with it, but helped lead in ways others couldn’t,” says Jeff Collins, president of advertising sales, marketing and brand partnerships for Fox Corp. Behind the scenes, his efforts held massive sway. The ad dollars he vetted helped the independent female-focused Oxygen cable network launch in 2000; boosted the presence of college football on ESPN; and lent support to new techniques to measure TV audiences that rely on whether viewers engage with what they watch, rather than how many people passively stare at whatever fills their screens. “John was always someone who understood the power of picking up the phone and saying, ‘I’ve got an idea for you. Would you be interested in hearing it?” says Ed Erhardt, who previously ran advertising sales for the entire ESPN portfolio at Disney. “Of course, we would always be interested in that.” And Muszynski did it all while Publicis grew, winning accounts from Anheuser-Busch InBev, Microsoft, Kenvue, Mars, Walmart, and, more recently, Pepsi. Publicis Media, for which Muszynski works, managed $62.4 billion worth of media spent around the world in 2025, according to COMvergence, a tracker of such activity. The figure marks a rise of 12.8%, or $7 billion, over what the company managed in 2024. Muszynski wasn’t the one charged with winning new accounts. Still, Publicis’ rise against competitors like WPP and Omnicom was fueled in part by Muszynski’s expertise, says Erhardt. “John Muszynski had a huge impact on that, his relationships with the sellers, but also the clients.” Whether the media companies liked all of Muszynski’s ideas or not, they had to listen to them. Those who didn’t agree might find some of their ad dollars going to a competitor. At a gathering of top TV sales executives in 2018, Muszynski was blunt. He cautioned the assemblage they might have to “deliver last year’s plan at the same budget, maybe less,” and warned them that the best way to win new ad dollars was to help advertisers bolster their sales. “All of you who are looking for increased budgets, the best way to do that is to help solve our clients’ problems,” he said at the time. Indeed, many companies have tried to do critical deals with Muszynski first. Because Publicis works on behalf of so many top advertisers, his take on the market is usually accurate. He often has a better sense than others of whether ad budgets are fat or lean. “We always arranged John’s deal first,” says Joe Abruzzese, who logged stints as the head of sales for CBS and Discovery Communications. “We really built our business on the way John was able to maneuver his clients.” In the yearly TV ad-sales market known as the “upfront, ” ad commitments don’t always end up in the bank. Advertisers may end up pulling the dollars they promised or asking for delays of their commercial orders. Not with Muszynski, say multiple sales executives. “John doesn’t over buy and then try to make it up,” says Charlie Collier, the media industry veteran who has worked in senior roles at Roku, Fox and AMC. “He has always been the guy who calls it like he sees it: ‘I’m not going promise all sorts of things that I then have to chase later. I’m going to tell you like I see it and make deals I know I can live up to.’ And he always did.” That trust in the way Muszynski conducted himself led to unorthodox negotiations. Abruzzese says he once convinced Muszynski to add $200 million to an “ upfront ” plan while sitting with him on the beach — and still has the piece of suntan-lotion-stained paper that displays the agreement. In another year, says Abruzzese, he and Muszynski worked out details on a tablecloth at a fancy dinner — and Muszynski had to pay the venue $50 so he could bring the linen back to his office where his colleagues could see the details. Such transactions have been going on for years. While working at Oxygen Media ahead of the launch of the network in 2000, says Collier, “We negotiated with him and he was terrific. We got a deal done. A few months later, he called: ‘You really screwed me!’ He had just picked up a client from another agency, and he thought the rates they had gotten were better. I said ‘They’re not. I remember this deal, and you came on with us in pre-launch, and we didn’t give someone more favorable terms.” To reassure Muszynski, says Collier, “I literally printed out our entire rate card, packaged it with women’s razors and products that were aimed at women, and put in a pink and blue box. I wrote, ‘You were good enough to come and support us in the early stages and here is our entire rate card.’ That’s the kind of trust I share with him. I don’t think I’ve sent a rate card to a client before or since.” Those sorts of exchanges are becoming less frequent. More advertisers use reams of algorithms and data brews to inform the way they spread their commercials across streaming outlets and FAST channels. Media-buying agencies and even legacy media companies have begun to tinker with the idea of letting AI find the right inventory and the best schedules on which commercials should run. Some marketing executives seem more interested in whether they can spur clicks to an Amazon cart or interactions with a QR code than they do in crafting a memorable piece of promotion that works because it was aligned with a particular program or media property. In an era that relies less on deals sealed with handshakes, Muszynski still had his clients’ confidence. But his successors may have a harder time winning it. The practice of figuring out how to place commercials and get a good price for them won’t collapse because of John Muszynski’s exit. Still, it might be left standing on shakier ground. title: ‘All Of A Sudden’ Wins Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Adolescence’ Breakout Owen Cooper Stars In New Beatles ‘In My Life’ Music Video ‘The List’ Author Yomi Adegoke Sets Audible Series ‘Playing The Game’ Rose Byrne To Head 2027 Tropfest Jury View All November 19, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'All of a Sudden' CineFrance, Bitters End EXCLUSIVE: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden has won the 2026 Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award , marking the first time a narrative feature has won the accolade. The finalists for the 2026 IFSN Advocate Award were Poh Si Teng’s American Doctor , Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me , Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA , Ross McElwee’s Remake , and Barbara Kopple’s Union Town . The IFSN award, created in 2022 to “highlight independent films each year that illuminate a humanitarian issue with a singular artistic vision,” comes with a singular prize for the winner: one million media impressions across the Indie Film Site Network, which represents The Film Stage, Hammer to Nail, IONCINEMA.com, Next Best Picture, RogerEbert.com, and Slant Magazine. Related Stories News Ryūsuke Hamaguchi's 'All Of A Sudden' To Open AFI Silver's 2026 European Union Film Showcase -- Full Lineup News Gotham Awards Film Nominations Led By 'The Invite', 'Tender Loving Care', 'All Of A Sudden' & More Previous IFSN Advocate Award winners include Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow ; Basel Adra, Hamdan Ballal, Yuval Abraham, and Rachel Szor’s No Other Land ; D. Smith’s Kokomo City ; and Shaunak Sen’s All That Breathes . Watch on Deadline “Bringing a staggering level of humanity and insight to life’s mysteries throughout his career, Ryusuke Hamaguchi has delivered his most universally empathetic film yet with All of a Sudden ,” Jordan Raup, co-founder of IFSN and editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Film Stage, said in a statement. “Led by luminous performances from Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto, this drama embodies everything the ideal IFSN Advocate Award encompasses: living everyday life with humble compassion toward anyone you encounter. That Hamaguchi also eloquently dissects how modern-era capitalism is rotting out the globe is nothing short of a miracle.” All of a Sudden premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, where Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto shared the Best Actress prize, and subsequently played at the Locarno Film Festival (where Virginie Efira received the honorary Leopard Club award), the Toronto International Film Festival, New York Film Festival, BFI London Film Festival, Chicago International Film Festival, where the film won the Silver Hugo for Best Screenplay, and the Montclair Film Festival, where the film won the Audience Award for World Cinema. The film is Japan’s entry for the 2027 Academy Awards and was nominated for four Gotham Awards, including Best International Feature, and a British Independent Film Award for Best International Independent Film. All of a Sudden opens in theaters on November 25 via Neon. title: Andrew Scott Has Thoughts About ‘Elsinore’, Life, Death & What Really Matters
full_text: I’m waiting for Andrew Scott in an LA restaurant on an unusually rainy afternoon, thinking about the last time we met, in 2024. Back then, as we’d chatted in the Deadline podcast studio, I’d asked him, “When was the last time you cried?” And he’d answered, simply, “Today.” It turned out his mother had died only a few days before. Terrified I’d made an awful time worse for him and wanting to offer support, I’d explained that my dad had passed a few months ago. Another actor might have quickly moved back to the safer topic of work — in this case, his role in the series Ripley — but instead, he’d asked, “How is it, further along?” Related Stories Festivals ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival Festivals ‘Elsinore’s Andrew Scott To Receive Palm Springs’ Desert Palm Achievement Award, Actor “You get more used to it,” I’d offered, lamely. Watch on Deadline There’s a quality to Scott that isn’t reserved for meeting him in person, he brings it to his work. And that is the sense that his feelings, the bald truth of his experiences, are right there on the surface, as though they involve us. So, when his latest film, Elsinore , premiered at Toronto, and Scott went deep into a story that skewers the preciousness of life, the inevitability of death and all of our collective losses, I, along with what seemed like the entire theater, simply dissolved . In the film, Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson — a man for whom the phrase ‘rage against the dying of the light’ might have been written. In 1989, when Charleson discovers he’s facing his own imminent death from AIDS-related illness, he’s offered his dream role, and deciding he’d “rather die of Hamlet than AIDS,” he takes to the stage in the ultimate act of defiance. Scott has been acting since he was eight years old. Ever since his mother, Nora, who was an art teacher, encouraged him to act as a way to get past shyness and a childhood lisp. A successful stage career followed, along with Spielberg’s TV miniseries Band of Brothers , a BAFTA-winning Sherlock role as Moriarty and a villain in the Bond film Spectre , among other things. But, it was, of course, Scott’s ‘hot priest’ in Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag that shot him to major stardom — it seemed everyone, including the critics, craved the forbidden fruit of his clergyman character. After that came Andrew Haigh’s All of Us Strangers opposite Paul Mescal and double Emmy nominations for the miniseries Ripley . But it’s the past two years, since I last saw him, that his head has to have truly been spinning. He’s taken on back-to-back jobs, like the film Blue Moon , Lena Dunham’s show Too Much, The Comeback with Lisa Kudrow, the films Wake Up Dead Man and Pressure, and the U.K. TV series It Gets Worse, in which he plays a bonkers therapist. Add to that the marathon of Vanya on stage in both London and Off-Broadway as a one-man show — that’s all five parts at once. Then, after Elsinore , he shot upcoming John Crowley-directed film Walk the Blue Fields with Emily Blunt and Ciarán Hinds. Plus Chloe Domont’s A Place in Hell with Michelle Williams and Daisy Edgar-Jones and Justine Triet’s psychological thriller Fonda. It’s a wonder he’s had any time to think… In Elsinore , under Simon Stone ’s direction and with Stephen Beresford ’s screenplay, Scott, who also serves as a producer, is joined by Olivia Colman as Ian’s physician Dr. Margaret Johnson, Billie Piper and Matthew Beard as Ian’s friends Patsy Pollock and Sean Mathias, Johnny Flynn as Hamlet director Richard Eyre , and such greats as Juliet Stevenson, who actually worked with Charleson in multiple stage productions, including The Taming of the Shrew in 1979. As Scott walks us through heart-piercing parallels between Ian and Hamlet, something like alchemy emerges — a sense that this is a film about all of us, in this moment. What really matters? What would we do, given just weeks to live? Back at the restaurant, Scott is suddenly standing there, wearing a cheerful sweatshirt with ‘P-Town’ across the front. He opens his arms to hug me, and I know then that he remembers the last time. What follows is a conversation about grief, the privilege and weight of getting older, how he plans to make the most of it, and why his favorite people live with courage and the daring “to say the unsayable.” DEADLINE: You are the same age as me. You recently turned 50, right? How do you feel about it? ANDREW SCOTT: I wasn’t looking forward to it. I don’t like my birthday anyway. DEADLINE: Why not? Just the fuss of it, you mean? SCOTT: I always like a sort of non-event, like the day after a wedding, or getting accidentally drunk on a Tuesday, rather than, “You’ve got this big thing.” They’re not necessarily as actually fun as you think they’re going to be. And then you’ve got big things like events with work and everything, that when it comes to my birthday, it feels like another thing to have to do, in some ways. I was working actually on my birthday. I was doing a play. I did this play Sea Wall in New York and I went out for dinner with friends and that was nice. What did you do? Did you do much? DEADLINE: I didn’t want to do anything, but then my friends were like, “Don’t be stupid. We are going to make you do something.” And it turned out to be the most amazing thing. SCOTT: Oh, really? Tell me more. DEADLINE: We rented a house together for a weekend. And it was incredible. SCOTT: Yeah, that’s what I’m going to do when things calm down. I’ve got to take my friends away. And that’s what I like. I did it for my 40th and my 45th. So, I’ll do it again. It’s gorgeous. I love, as my sister calls it, ‘the long hang.’ Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in ‘Elsinore’ Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC DEADLINE: It’s a bit like getting married, these birthdays. You have this leverage to make people go somewhere and do something. SCOTT: Yeah, exactly. I just love the idea you get all the new stuff out of the way and then you’re just into having a laugh with people. Just talking and going home and having a drink. DEADLINE: When I first saw Elsinore , I did that kind of crying where you feel like your chest hurts. I could not get it together. Red, puffy, blubbering. I thought, OK the second time I watch this film, I’ll be fine. SCOTT: Because you know what’s coming. DEADLINE: Nope. Absolute carnage, just a total mess. I also experienced it with our last meeting in mind. SCOTT: Yes, I remember so well. DEADLINE: Meeting you was the first time that someone had asked me what grief is like a little bit further down the road, because it was so new to me. And I would now say to you that it gets worse. SCOTT: [Laughs] Yeah, it gets worse. Scott as Ian in ‘Elsinore’ Anthony Dickenson / Focus Features/STUDIOCANAL DEADLINE: The film had such a profound effect on me. Watching Ian really go for his life’s dream against the clock at only 40 is devastating and glorious at the same time. And being 50 now, it’s also because it’s the turning point where you start thinking, oh, sh*t. SCOTT: Yeah, absolutely. You think you just have an awareness of the value of time. And I think it’s actually what the film is about. It’s about our most valuable asset, which is our time. And what Ian chose to do with it, he chose that he was going to choose quality over quantity, and that actually, this lifelong goal that he had just came right when his taxi was waiting, so to speak. And he got to do this thing right at the very end of the finish line. And that, I think, really affects people. My friend has this great expression, which is ‘little did we know.’ She was like, “Little do we know. We don’t know what way it’s going to go.” Little do we know what’s going to happen to us this evening. At the end of every day, you’re able to go, “God, I have no idea that that’s what’s going to happen.” And something new does happen every single day if you choose to keep your antennae on. And I think Ian was very aware that he wanted something new, because I think one of the most insidious things about being ill, as we know, is being in a hospital, waiting outside in waiting rooms, and waiting for results, and lethargy in some ways. So, he used to go to the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, then down to rehearsal, where you are exploring the greatest play that has ever been written about life and death, playing that extraordinary part with these brilliant artists. I mean, in some ways, of course you want to do that. And so, even though people thought that it was going to be the destruction of him, in some ways I think he thought it was going to heal him. And it did, in some ways. You go, “I’m going to do this, because time is a-marching on.” And if not now, when? If not now, when? And is there going to be a project which I feel more passionate than this? I don’t think so. Andrew Scott There is another thing they call Dr. Theater, which is a thing where you might have a terrible cold and you’re in such a bad mood. You come in and you’re like, “Oh my god, I’m not going to be able to do it.” And then you go on and you do the play. It’s something about the collective imagination of the audience. They don’t care about your cold. They don’t care about anything else. Plus your imagination and plus the story from start to finish being said in the dark, that your cold and your bad feeling, you just go to a place and you don’t feel ill for that time that you’re on stage and then you come off and you… DEADLINE: … puke in a bucket like Ian did. SCOTT: Exactly. And it’s true. I think any actor, particularly in the theater, will tell you about Dr. Theater. DEADLINE: I’ve been listening to the audio version of Judi Dench’s memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It? In it she talks having to pretend to drink on the stage. Obviously, it’s just colored water, but she felt so drunk by the end of it. Have you ever felt like that? The crowd making you feel it? SCOTT: Yeah. It’s definitely a thing, isn’t it? It makes you think about the energy of the people that you have in your life and how you break free of things that are just not giving you anything, like this [points to iphone on the table]. That’s one thing I think an awful lot about. DEADLINE: Yes, my hand is always reaching for the dopamine hit of the phone. SCOTT: All the time. Sometimes before you’re even awake, you have somebody telling you about peptides or micronutrients. Do you know what I mean? Just stuff that you’re like, “Whoa.” That’s what anxiety is — receiving so much information about which you can do very little. That’s actually literally kind of textbook anxiety. It’s just a time stealer. That’s the biggest thing. It’s a time stealer and it’s not rest. It seems like rest, but it’s not. Scott as Ian Charleson with Olivia Colman as Dr. Margaret Johnson Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC DEADLINE: What’s it like for you to watch this film? Are you able to watch it in an objective way, or is that impossible for you? Is it difficult emotionally? SCOTT: I do feel emotional about it. I won’t watch it anymore. I’ve seen it enough now. I wanted to see it with an audience. Obviously, I saw cuts of it [before]. Telluride was the first time I saw it. It is difficult to watch, yeah. I never watched the dailies on set when I’m acting, because it’s so distracting in some ways. Sometimes I would watch it to see what the frame might be, but I never look at it in relation to the performance. But actually I really, really immersed myself in it more than ever. I always do a little bit, but this one was so intense. It was a quick shoot for what we had to cover comparatively. I think it was maybe six weeks. It’s a lot. And Ian was in every single scene. And there’s so many beats you have to hit in some ways, and the performance, and the tracking of his illness. And some days, because of the constraints of the budget, you have to be ill in the morning and healthy in the afternoon. And your appearance was changing, which could be difficult, but it meant that we were able to get the actors that we wanted, rather than schedule it out so that it would be easy. If we were going to get Olivia Colman or we were going to get Billie or Johnny Flynn or whoever, we’d prioritize getting them, and so we would get the actors when we needed them. And if that meant we had to change rather than just doing a chronological decline, so to speak, that’s what we tried to do. So, I decided that I was going to make it fun, trying to make it fun, because one of the things about Ian was that he was enormously fun kind of guy. It’s what everybody said about him. DEADLINE: You learned that from his family and friends? SCOTT: Yeah. Everybody who encountered him, that’s what the first thing they’d say, that he was very sparkly and kind of flirtatious and just had a great sense of humor. And it was a tough road to get the film made as it is. So, actually just being on set, I was just delighted to be there. I was like, “Yes, this is happening. Here everybody is.” The last time we spoke was just after mum died and it definitely, without a doubt, fueled the passion behind this project. There’s no doubt about it. It occurred to me, as we were moving on with the development of the film, that I was really, really attached to it, because there were so many things in it that I felt I could relate to about mortality and about identity, sexual and otherwise. Shakespeare, the theater, The National Theatre, actors, love, all those things. And so, I just got more and more involved in it. Even though I feel a little bit heartbroken that mum isn’t here to watch it, because she’d be so proud and she’d love it. In some ways, I don’t think going into studios and into financiers, I can remember that now. I was a man on a mission, because I feel like when you have a loss like that, as you know, you have nothing else to lose. DEADLINE: You’ve got to keep moving too. SCOTT: You go, “I’m going to do this, because time is a-marching on.” And if not now, when? If not now, when? And is there going to be a project which I feel more passionate than this? I don’t think so — you can say, “little do I know,” but certainly up ‘til now. And then you watch it and you go “Ok that’s quite a lot.” But I enjoyed it in some ways. After we’d do big, long days, and because there was a certain weight, frankly, that I had to be at, I used to go to the gym in the evening. I used to walk home, because on sets you don’t move. I used to walk home and then I would learn whatever soliloquy or whatever it was on the way home. And even though it was incredibly intense in the middle of the winter, there’s something where you just go, “I’m going to immerse myself in this and pretty much this alone.” It’s a kind of privilege to be able to get to do that. L to R: Billie Piper, director Simon Stone, Olivia Colman, DP Mike Eley and Johnny Flynn on the set of ‘Elsinore’. Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC DEADLINE: I was speaking to a friend recently about how work can very easily become our whole lives, and I was thinking about that Mary Oliver quote, “Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?” And the idea of, did anyone on their deathbed ever wish they’d worked more, rather than loved more or had more fun? But then I thought, actually Ian did, because work seems like a vocation for him. Is it like that for you? SCOTT: Sometimes it’s vocational. And I think it’s really interesting to hear you say that. There are certain projects that are vocational and there are certain things, certainly over the past couple of years, where I think I’ve used work to keep my head afloat. One, there were certain financial obligations that I have in my family that I want to honor and all that stuff, and two, because it gives you structure. After I did Elsinore, I made another film and there was a lot of work around that time. DEADLINE: Walk the Blue Fields with Emily Blunt? SCOTT: Yeah [laughs. I can’t say her name without laughing, because she’s so much fun. She just sent me a hysterical voice note. Isn’t that the power of Emily Blunt? Say her name and I start to laugh. But anyway, you have to start thinking as my birthday approached and all that stuff, you think, “OK, but what else? What are the other things that you could apply this kind of energy to your life?” And not everything can be vocational. Doing a job like Elsinore has to affect your health in some ways. Or doing plays like Vanya . I never really stopped all that time. And after I did Vanya actually, I was unwell after that for a while. I had to affect having a panic attack in that play. For about the last two weeks of the run, I started [having panic attacks for real]. For about six weeks after, I thought, wow, your body just doesn’t know the difference. So, to unlearn it, I was checking my [heart rate]. I got an Apple watch. I don’t know if you ever had a panic attack, but it feels like you’re going to have a heart attack, and then you check your [vitals], and you go, “No, that’s not happening. That’s not happening.” Scott as Ian Charleson and Joe Locke as Nicholas dancing to ‘The Ethel Merman Disco Album’ in ‘Elsinore’. Focus Features / Focus Features/STUDIOCANAL SCOTT: [The waiter hands him the protein smoothie he ordered.] Thank you. Back in the day we’d be having a martini. DEADLINE: What’s happened to us? SCOTT: I know. So, anyway, yeah, what you say about vocation is really true. And I do feel that. I do feel like some things, those things, will really light you up. I’m pretty good at making the wildness of this job, and the travel, and the jet lag, and the endlessness of it, trying to see the fun of it, because it is fun. DEADLINE: The reality is though that you are constantly on the move and dealing with jetlag… SCOTT: And then they just paint you and they push you on the red carpet [laughs]. God knows, I’m not complaining. I’m really not. My god. You do think, this is fun. And because as an actor, you want to take your opportunities, this is bliss. And actually, when I was really exhausted coming from Elsinore , I remember arriving in Dublin. I’d been to the South by Southwest Festival in Austin, Texas and I came back and went to rehearse with Emily in Dublin. The costume designer told me weeks later, “I sort of exhaled and inhaled, because you just looked so awful.” And it was because I just hadn’t slept or whatever. But then you go and you start working with divine people like Emily Blunt and Ciarán Hines and John Crowley. I just had a ball. I love the idea that acting is of use to people, that for people who can’t express themselves that way, someone else will do that, and will be vulnerable in front of 1,000 people in order to do something that I think is a service in the world. Of course, it’s not rocket science, but it isn’t meaningless and it is a great use to people. Andrew Scott DEADLINE: I’m looking forward to seeing that. SCOTT: Emily is a very, very special person. Have you met her? DEADLINE: Yes. I love her humor. Watching Elsinore, I get this massive bolt of nostalgia being British, because British people, and, not to speak for you, but I think Irish people too, have such a thing for undercutting sadness with humor, it’s Fleaba g humor. It’s the way that Ian talks and there’s always this thing of, “Don’t get too sad, because I’m going to hit you with something rude.” And Emily’s humor… SCOTT: …is exactly like that. Sometimes the kindest thing you can do when someone gives you bad news is not to give them a hug. The kindest, most sensitive thing to do is to make fun of them.That’s why I love Stephen’s script. When Ian comes out to the company [telling them he has AIDS], they say, “Well, you’re the only person in the company who hasn’t bought any biscuits.”That’s so great. What a line. And, “You’re always drawing attention to yourself.” And then everybody’s always laughing, because it’s so wildly inappropriate. I love the daring of that. I love that that is what actors are like. All the best people in my life, in fact, I think the loves of my life really, have been people like that, that dare to say the unsayable and are courageous in that way. Acting is a much-derided profession and sometimes quite rightly, but I love the idea that acting is of use to people, that for people who can’t express themselves that way, someone else will do that, and will be vulnerable in front of 1,000 people in order to do something that I think is a service in the world. Of course, it’s not rocket science, but it isn’t meaningless and it is a great use to people. Scott as Ian rehearsing ‘Hamlet’ in ‘Elsinore’. Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC DEADLINE: I think the only thing that truly changes people’s minds is art and storytelling. SCOTT: I totally agree. And I always think of during the pandemic, the first thing we went to was the arts. What are you listening to? What boxset are you watching? What film are you watching? What book are you reading? That’s why it’s got to be treated seriously. That’s why it should be for everybody. DEADLINE: Doing the press for this film, of course people want you to compare your experience as a gay actor now, given that Ian’s career would have, in 1989, potentially been torpedoed by coming out. That’s a big part of his story in Elsinore , including where Derek Jarman, played by David Dawson, takes issue with his decision not to come out. Nobody would ever want to be dismissive of how that would have felt for Ian and the reality of that, but now, is there a time when we can stop pointing to a person’s sexuality? Do you know what I’m saying? SCOTT: Well, the idea of modernity, the idea that we have to get with it, because it’s 2026, like it’s an iPhone update. Because in 1976 we could be forgiven for being old-fashioned? Or in 1856? As if different forms of human sexuality have not existed since the dawn of humanity, and will continue to the end of humanity. So, we’re going, “OK, well, I think I better update my attitudes towards sexuality, because it’s 2029.” It’s sort of like, “I’m now going to accept green eyes.” I don’t know, there’s a degree of preposterousness to it. But having said that, I do feel proud and grateful that I have experienced change, albeit a slow-moving change, in our industry. I don’t think that I would’ve got a chance to play this part. I don’t know. But I do find it a little… It can be reductive just talking about that, as if there’s no acting required or skill required to imagine how somebody with the same sexuality as you would be. DEADLINE: No one would apply that to a straight person playing another straight person. SCOTT: Exactly, yeah. Actually, maybe one of the things that in some ways I’m happy to talk about is, there probably would’ve been a time maybe 20 years ago that that would’ve been a concern. But actually, the thing that I feel liberated from is that I have the right to play lots of different parts and I am going to continue to do that. And if I don’t get a part like that in movies or whatever, I will do in the theater, or I’ll do something else. I feel like I have experience in having gone through all the bits, the parts, where I felt fearful of that and I felt like, oh, maybe not talking about that will disappear that subject. And now I feel like I have some degree of authority or experience about that subject, maybe as much as anybody else. So, why shouldn’t I, in some ways, have a conversation about it, that I don’t necessarily know the answers to? And that’s maybe the insidious thing about talking about the media, is that you can’t ask a question. You seem to always have to be providing the answer. I think Stephen [Beresford] writes love unlike anybody else, because there’s a sort of brutality to it. The relationship between Dr. Margaret Johnson and Ian, Olivia and me, they’re not warm or lovey with each other. In fact, they’re quite antagonistic. And that allows the audience to search for the love. Andrew Scott DEADLINE: At the London Film Festival, you had this incredible screening where you brought onto the stage some of the real-life people from this story. Including Ian’s doctor, Dr. Margaret Johnson, who did so much incredible, groundbreaking work in the fight against HIV and AIDS. You had her on-screen counterpart Olivia Colman bring her on stage to a standing ovation. And Ian’s sister, Lizzie was there, and Ralph Mills, the wardrobe technician from The National Theatre was brought on stage by Paul Chahidi, who played him. And then there was Monica Dolan and the woman she played, Linda Tolhurst, the keeper of the theatre’s backstage entrance. SCOTT: Yes. She’s been at The National for 46 years. DEADLINE: What was that like for you? SCOTT: If I’m honest, I wanted to orchestrate that entire thing. I wanted that to happen. I was pretty adamant that that’s what we’re going to do. And luckily everybody around was in agreement, because Margaret is not a public person, but to see 2,000 people stand up and give her the due that she deserved was so extraordinary. It was really, really special to have Linda and Sean Mathias, who was one of Ian’s best friends, that Matthew Beard plays in the movie. Lizzie is Ian’s absolutely beautiful sister. All Ian’s family were there. So, many friends and family flew in. It was a genuinely special night. And then we played the Ethel Merman song [“There’s No Business Like Show Business” from The Ethel Merman Disco Album that Ian played on the hospital ward in the film]. Dr. Margaret Johnson and Olivia Colman on stage at the ‘Elsinore’ opening gala at the BFI London Film Festival. Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images for BFI For some reason, I was obsessed with the idea. There’s something about curtain calls in life that is very pleasing for an audience, that we give people their due. Only actors get a curtain call. And it felt like, in a film about theater, that the real people should have a curtain call. It gives the audience a chance to express their appreciation and hopefully for them to realize that what they’ve done is so remarkable. So, it was really special. And to do it at the BFI, which was 30 seconds from The National Theatre. I’ve got to say, it took a real team of really brilliant people. DEADLINE: Does anything of Ian stay with you? Because obviously for your own mental health, you can’t always be carrying around your characters. SCOTT: I think, because I’ve been working as an actor for such a long time, I’ve got really used to it. and he just really loved it so much. And I’ve never been complacent about it, I wouldn’t say that at all. But he was very proud of being an actor and I think that’s a nice thing to hold onto. It’s not that I’m questioning of it, because I still really enjoy it, but I want to hold onto my feeling of gratitude. But actually, in order to do that… I’ve got this bag of work that I’ve done that’s going to come out in the next year. Andrew Scott, Linda Tolhurst and Monica Dolan on stage after the ‘Elsinore’ BFI London Film Festival opening gala. Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images for BFI DEADLINE: Are you thinking of taking a break? SCOTT: I do really want to. I’m in a place where I really feel like I can, for lots of different reasons. And I think I’m ready to stop, since the first chokehold of grief has subsided a little bit, or at least I’m used to it. I think I can afford to listen to the silence. DEADLINE: To sit with yourself? SCOTT: …to sit with yourself! Arghhhhh! DEADLINE: Right, it’s like “Quick! Turn on the telly!” SCOTT: Yes. [Laughs] DEADLINE : Our columnist Baz Bamigboye recently did an interview with Elsinore producer Gabrielle Tana and she was talking about how in the early days of this idea, it was maybe going to be about a road trip that Ian does with his friend, the filmmaker Ethan Silverman. And then Stephen Beresford evolved it into Ian’s experience playing Hamlet . Were you willing to play Ian even if it was a totally different story, on that road trip? SCOTT: I wouldn’t say that. I would say there were a couple of ideas about what Ian’s story would be. There was an idea of a story of him taking a road trip in Italy. And then Stephen started to research the idea, and they approached him about writing a screenplay with the idea of me playing Ian. And obviously Stephen, I’m worked with him so many times and I know his voice, so no better person… I would’ve gone where Stephen went and Stephen never really went on the road trip. And then, as you say, when you found gold, you can’t go back. And he really is the reason why the film, I think, is… There are so many things that are about Ian, but also Stephen’s giant-heartedness is the reason that this film works, and Stephen’s sense of humor and Stephen’s experience as an actor, and his understanding of what I think I’m able to do, what I think is my understanding of how he writes. I think Stephen writes love unlike anybody else, because there’s a sort of brutality to it. The relationship between Dr. Margaret Johnson and Ian, Olivia and me, they’re not warm or lovey with each other. In fact, they’re quite antagonistic. And that allows the audience to search for the love. DEADLINE: Yes. When she finally goes to see him play Hamlet and there are tears in her eyes, but she doesn’t say anything to him later. There’s a space for us to fill in what passed between them. SCOTT: Totally. And when Patsy says, “If you think I’m not the kind of person who’s going to beat down the door…” DEADLINE: “…then you haven’t been paying attention, darling.” SCOTT: Or when Linda says, “Don’t die on me,” and Ian goes, “Tell her to mind her own business.” I love all that, because it’s still affection. And I think that’s very sophisticated, actually. Johnny Flynn as Richard Eyre and Billie Piper as Patsy Pollock in ‘Elsinore’. Anthony Dickenson / Focus Features/STUDIOCANAL DEADLINE: And of course there are all the parallels with the Shakespeare text. When Ian’s saying goodbye to his friend and ex-lover Georgie [Luke Thompson] and then almost straight afterwards we go to Ian rehearsing Hamlet, holding the skull, doing the “Alas, poor Yorick” scene. As a producer on this, having yourself performed Hamlet 150 times in 2017 at the Almeida Theatre, how much did you and Stephen go back and forth on which passages from Hamlet worked best? SCOTT: Yes. Yeah, that was a big, big, big thing. We sifted through the script to see which bits would be… You have to present Hamlet in some ways, not like the greatest hits of Hamlet , but when we think of Hamlet , what do we think of? We think of the skull and we think of the sword fight and we think of, “To be, or not to be.” But that thing, “I see the imminent death of 20,000 men,” that really hit me, that was written 400 years ago. And he’s like, the injustice of that. They “go to their graves like beds”. And Simon Stone’s really terrific about that and he understands dramaturgy expertly. I love all that stuff. And Simon and Stephen and I really collaborated very, very closely on all that stuff. DEADLINE: On that Mary Oliver thing and about being 50, what is playing on your mind as things that you want to get done? It’s hard to know in advance, but Ian knew — the time was now and the opportunity was now. Someone once asked me when I was a kid trying to figure out what I wanted to do, “If you were dying, what would you be upset that you hadn’t done?” SCOTT: In a way, I’ve been focused a lot of my life in getting things done. And I actually think the bigger question is what do I want to be? Because it’s like that expression, to stop the glorification of busy. That’s not to dismiss the question, but if you’re able to even appreciate being exhausted and go, “OK, I’m doing this, this is what I’m doing, and this is going to end.” You know what I mean? A problem about being exhausted is that you lose your perspective. If you don’t have a day off. I had a period where I had five weeks where I didn’t have any day off at all. I was starting to go dark and I thought, I’m not doing that anymore. I’ve got to be able to say no, and that’s a kindness to myself and actually to other people. It’s not necessary. So, actually in some ways, for me, it’s about trying to do less. I think it’s to do less, or at least to experiment with that for a while, because it’s f**king scary a little bit for me to do less. Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC DEADLINE: What does doing less look like for you? SCOTT: It’s only the period of my life that I feel now, because I have done a lot of work in the past year or two. And so, the seesaw is just a bit that way. So, I just need to give myself space to… I’ve spent an awful lot of time in New York in the past. Such a brilliant place. I love it so much. It’s been really, really healing for me, because I think I want to be a person that’s in nature all the time, but I’m not. I love nature, god, don’t get me wrong, but there is part of me that has an energy that responds to cities. And rest is sometimes going out dancing, that’s what it is. What if I’m one of the people that is able to stay a bit later, or able to go, “Oh yeah, I will go away for the weekend,” or, “I am able to go to your wedding.” DEADLINE: I hope you get to go out in LA and have some fun. Maybe pop across the road to the Chateau Marmont? SCOTT: I love the Sunset Tower [hotel bar]. I love the fact that you go in there and you can’t see a f**king thing. You know that they say that’s how you know you’re in a gay man’s apartment, because you can’t see sh*t. DEADLINE: Lighting has to be flattering. SCOTT: Exactly. Let the skin glow. DEADLINE: My friend loves pink light bulbs. You can’t get those in LA anymore. They’re all LEDs now. SCOTT: LED is absolutely disgusting. It’s like high-def television. Violent. DEADLINE: So now we can all look old together. Focus Features will open Elsinore in select U.S. theaters on November 20, expanding to additional markets from December 4. StudioCanal releases Elsinore in U.K. cinemas on January 29, 2027. SHOOT: Director, DP and editor: Sela Shiloni; 1st assistant: Morgan Demeter; 2nd assistant: Jack Morris. ANDREW SCOTT’S LOOK: Styling by Warren Alfie Baker; clothing by Ferragamo. MUSIC: “Call to Stage” from the Elsinore soundtrack, written by Elsinore composer Stefan Gregory and released by Back Lot Music. Performed by Ben Dawson on solo piano with the London Contemporary Orchestra, under conductor Hugh Tieppo. Read More About: Comments

title: ‘I, Daniel Blake’ Producer Says She Is “Bored Of Seeing Same Faces On Screen” As She Sets Out Blueprint To Revitalize Indie Movie Sector
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Biggest ITV Shows Like ‘Love Island’ & ‘I’m A Celebrity’ To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of “Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States” On UK Audiences Melissa George Leading BBC-BritBox Detective Series ‘The Loch Ness Mysteries’ View All November 19, 2026 8:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'I, Daniel Blake' Sixteen Films Rebecca O’Brien, Ken Loach ’s BAFTA-winning producing partner, has said she is “bored of seeing the same faces on screen” in lower budget movies. Delivering the Lord Richard Attenborough Memorial Address at the British Screen Forum Conference, O’Brien set out a blueprint to revitalize the indie movie sector and allow movies like Loach’s to continue to flourish. With Loach she runs Sixteen Films, and has made more than a dozen indie movies with the celebrated director. “We need funders to be more open to casting from a wider pool,” she said. “Casting super famous actors is great but it’s a myth that the marquee value is everything. I’m bored of seeing the same faces on screen. It homogenizes and unbalances these lower budget films.” Related Stories News Biggest ITV Shows Like 'Love Island' & 'I'm A Celebrity' To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes News BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of "Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States" On UK Audiences O’Brien stressed she is “not anti-actor” but said too many stars now “believe they can increase their influence and power by becoming producers.” “Yes, it’s great to develop your own projects but when it comes to actually getting them made, most actors don’t always know how to do the job of making a film,” she added. “Why should they?” Watch on Deadline At the same time, O’Brien raised concerns that talented up-and-coming British filmmakers are “often siphoned off, sometimes too soon and over-optimistically, into the studio system.” “So now, with less funding, the independent sector has ended up becoming the research and development wing of the film industry in this country.” On this, she pointed to the growing microdrama space as being full of “fresh voices trying to find a way to burst out.” O’Brien said too many indie movies are getting made without ambitions of making serious money, as the I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley producer called on funders to “say no more clearly.” “Too many projects that frankly aren’t good enough get made,” she added. “A direct no is far more helpful than a maybe and it’s useful to have cogent reasoning as to why it’s not going to make the grade.” She said the “brutal truth” in the “diminishing” indie movie market is that “a film must have genuine theatrical potential for distributors to be interested.” O’Brien calls for quotas O’Brien’s blueprint involves serious consideration of “quotas purely for domestic [British] films on streaming and pay TV services,” which is “at the heart of the market failure for the sector.” She also called for financing these smaller projects to become less complex so that she doesn’t end up “being on a Zoom with 20 lawyers bickering over the recoupment schedule.” “We need to find ways in which to enable the next generations to tell their stories,” she said, passionately. “With some structural changes and simplifications, some slimming down and some radical thinking, we can boost and recharge the sector. With the right wind in its sails a small film can punch way above its weight and benefit the whole industry.” O’Brien harked back to a “chamber piece that was simple and manageable,” her and Loach’s Palme d’Or winning I, Daniel Blake . “With enlightened funders who left us to get on with the job, creative, engaged distribution and sales partners and an audience who saw themselves reflected on the screen in this little story, we achieved a lot,” she added. “That’s what we’re asking for.” Disney+’s ‘Afterlife With Archie’ Casts Archie, Veronica, Betty, Jughead & Sabrina Comcast & Skydance Shut Euro Streamer SkyShowtime; CEO Exiting Netflix, Penélope Cruz & Director Juan Diego Botto Begin ‘Patricia’ Warner Bros TV & Paramount TV Studios To Merge Under Dungey & Thunell Read More About: Comments

title: Tilly Norwood Creator Teases Next Project ‘Storm Dogs’ & Shows Clip
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘I, Daniel Blake’ Producer Says She Is “Bored Of Seeing Same Faces On Screen” As She Sets Out Blueprint To Revitalize Indie Movie Sector Biggest ITV Shows Like ‘Love Island’ & ‘I’m A Celebrity’ To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of “Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States” On UK Audiences View All November 19, 2026 2:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tilly Norwood Particle 6 The creator of controversial AI actor Tilly Norwood has teased her next project with Lion King co-director Rob Minkoff . The audience at today’s British Screen Forum Conference in London were treated to a clip of Storm Dogs , as Eline Van der Velden took them behind the scenes of the making of the AI-assisted movie, first revealed by Deadline a few weeks back. Van der Velden, who runs the film’s production company Particle6, said the movie mixes real actors with some AI. Having AI actors play toddlers and dogs made life easier on set, she joked. Related Stories News UK Culture Minister Delivers Emotional Plea To YouTube To "Set An Example" & Remove Russell Brand's Channel News SAG-AFTRA Boss Says AI Takedowns Matter More Than Damages To Performers She also said her team had built a tech platform made “by creatives for creatives” to help produce the film. Watch on Deadline “It’s really hard to do AI well, that’s why there is so much slop,” said Van der Velden. “AI might reduce your budget by 50% but it won’t go to 0%. That’s why you’ve not seen a good AI feature yet.” She is confident Storm Dogs, which counts Minkoff at the helm, can buck the trend. Van der Velden said her team is “pushing to get real actors back on screen even in this new medium,” while Particle6 has given jobs to 30 budding filmmakers in the past year. “I believe the industry will grow as a result of this technology,” she added. “Brands will want to come in, looking to be the next Mattel. It’s not dissimilar from the 1920s when the talkies came in.” Tilly “succeeded in sparking a debate” Van der Velden reflecting on a year in which her controversial AI creation Norwood has dominated chatter around AI and the industry. Norwood “succeeded in sparking a debate” about rules and regulation around industry AI, she said. “She really cut through the noise,” added Van der Velden. “She embodied the fear we’re all feeling when it comes to AI.” Van der Velden, who is an actor herself, said Norwood was an “interesting experiment to see how my skills as an actor would translate in this new medium.” “Tilly is me, I am Tilly,” she added. Van der Velden was speaking at the British Screen Forum after former Amazon UK boss Chris Bird, who now runs AI venture Hawkshead . title: Comcast And Skydance Shuttering European Streamer SkyShowtime; CEO Monty Sarhan Exiting
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Netflix Animated Series ‘Living The Dream’ Gets Trailer & Release Date Comcast And Skydance Shuttering European Streamer SkyShowtime; CEO Monty Sarhan Exiting ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’: Could Video Game Franchise Become Film Or TV Show? “We’re Very, Very Selective,” Says Take-Two CEO View All November 19, 2026 2:20am Add us as a Google Preferred Source SkyShowtime SkyShowtime SkyShowtime ‘s lifespan is officially coming to an end. The European streaming service will close its doors at the end of 2027, with CEO Monty Sarhan leaving as part of the move. SkyShowtime’s CFO, Mark Neil, will become interim General Manager as the company winds down. Staff were informed of the official decision to close in an internal note from the board of directors this week. The writing had been on the wall for the Comcast and Skydance -backed service since it emerged two months ago that a strategic review was underway, with options including winding down on the table. Related Stories Executives David Ellison Goes Personal: Raised By Single Mom, Bonded With Dad As Teen, Massive VHS Collection Executives Skydance Chief Marketing Officer Rebecca Mall Sets Leadership Team, WBD's Meg Maro To Depart It’s understood shareholders were concerned that SkyShowtime had not turned a profit despite a huge spend on content. Last year, Deadline revealed had invested at least $1B into the service, but it had remained solidly in the red, and ongoing speculation this year suggested that had not changed. Watch on Deadline The board appeared to confirm this in its letter to staff. “Since SkyShowtime’s launch, the streaming landscape has evolved significantly,” it read. “Major global platforms have continued to expand their scale and invest heavily in content, technology, and sport. “These competitive dynamics have made it increasingly challenging for regional players like SkyShowtime to achieve the scale needed for long-term success. Despite the excellent work and dedication of this team, the shareholders have determined that winding down the business is the most appropriate path forward.” SkyShowtime was launched in 2022 out of Amsterdam as a JV streaming service between Paramount , then ViacomCBS, and Comcast as a way of entering European territories that didn’t have access to their own streamers Paramount+ or Peacock. It combines shows from those two streamers plus Sky Studios and local originals, and has subscribers across 22 European markets. However, the service is operating in a different landscape to its pandemic era roots, with Paramount now sitting inside the same Skydance tent as Warner Bros. Discovery and Comcast splitting its entertainment services up, with cable networks business Versant now separate to NBCUniversal. UK pay TV business Sky handles Comcast’s investment in SkyShowtime. Here’s the letter from the board in full. Dear SkyShowtime Employees, In September, we shared that SkyShowtime’s shareholders had initiated a review of strategic options, followed by the start of employee consultations in October. That review has now concluded, and the shareholders have made the decision to wind down SkyShowtime’s operations in late 2027. Since SkyShowtime’s launch, the streaming landscape has evolved significantly. Major global platforms have continued to expand their scale and invest heavily in content, technology, and sport. These competitive dynamics have made it increasingly challenging for regional players like SkyShowtime to achieve the scale needed for long-term success. Despite the excellent work and dedication of this team, the shareholders have determined that winding down the business is the most appropriate path forward. After over four years leading the SkyShowtime business, Monty Sarhan has agreed with the Board that it is an appropriate time to exit the company. We thank Monty for his commitment and contributions to SkyShowtime’s journey. We are also grateful to Mark Neil, who has agreed to serve as Interim General Manager, overseeing the wind-down operating period. We are committed to supporting everyone at SkyShowtime throughout this process and sharing information as decisions are implemented. In the meantime, SkyShowtime continues to operate as normal for our members. Employee consultations remain ongoing in accordance with local requirements, and timing and process may vary by country. We want to thank each of you for your hard work, professionalism, and commitment to SkyShowtime and its members. We are grateful for your contributions and will keep you informed as we move forward. Presenting an episode of their Sunday Service show, Laura Brand delivered some words on behalf of her husband, who is behind bars in Littlehey Prison, a jail for men who have been convicted of sexual offenses. Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Reading from a notepad, Laura Brand said: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.” Related Stories News UK Culture Minister Delivers Emotional Plea To YouTube To "Set An Example" & Remove Russell Brand's Channel News YouTube Investigating Russell Brand Prison Message Video She continued: “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. Watch on Deadline “The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone. “I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.” An audibly emotional Laura Brand added: “Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell.” Laura opened the YouTube video by saying that she was streaming to “continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday Service community. Something very, very close to mine and Russell’s heart.” Earlier over the weekend, one of Brand‘s accusers waived her legal right to anonymity after the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star was imprisoned. In an interview with The Sunday Times , Mia Latter alleged that she was orally raped by Brand in 2006, when she was aged 16 and he was 30. She alleged that Brand referred to her as “the child” during their relationship, which she now considers to have been emotionally and sexually abusive. title: Senate And House Lawmakers Added As Cosponsors To New Federal Film & TV Incentive Legislation
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Senate And House Lawmakers Added As Cosponsors To New Federal Film & TV Incentive Legislation Newsmax Files Antitrust Lawsuit Against Fox Corp. Over Roku Acquisition David Ellison Says There Might Be “Some News Sharing In The Future” Between CBS And CNN View All November 19, 2026 3:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Al Drago/Getty Images UPDATED, with coalition letter: More than 60 House members and four Senators have signed on to legislation to establish a 20% federal film incentive, amid an effort to see passage during the lame duck session of Congress . The new cosponsors in the Senate include Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC), Sen. Katie Britt (R-AL) and Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL). On the House side, boosters pointed to a long list of new co-sponsors that include Democrats such as Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-WA) and Rep. Josh Gottheimer, and Republicans such as Rep. Ken Calvert (R-CA) and Rep. Vince Fong (R-CA). Related Stories News Elon Musk Feels "Pretty Foolish" For Donating Mega-Bucks To Losing MAGA In Midterms News Newsmax Files Antitrust Lawsuit Against Fox Corp. Over Roku Acquisition The legislation, the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act , was introduced in September by Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) and, in the House, by Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Rep. Linda Sánchez (D-CA), Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) and Laura Friedman (D-CA). Watch on Deadline The prospects for passage during the lame duck appear to hinge on attaching the legislation to a year-end funding bill or tax legislation, rather than as a standalone measure. A challenge has been the set of priorities of Republicans in their waning weeks in the leadership, with the Senate devoting substantial floor time to getting through President Donald Trump ‘s nominees. Trump announced last summer that he is backing the legislation, giving the long gestating proposal a boost. Following the Republicans’ midterm drubbing, Trump has tried to give the bill’s prospects a boost by urging lawmakers to “get this done” in a social media post. This week, industry representatives have been lobbying Congress, including SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin, who met with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA), House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-MA) and Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO), the chairman of the House Ways & Means Committee, among others. The bill also has the recently announced support of groups including the AFL-CIO, American Hotel and Lodging Association, the American Entertainment Alliance, The Internet and Television Association, and the Laborers’ International Union of North America. The group Collective Moxie also led a coalition letter urging members of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus, Congressional Black Caucus, Congressional Hispanic Caucus and Congressional Native American Caucus to pass the incentive. The letter was signed by more than 200 organizations and individuals who have advocated for inclusive and diverse storytelling. Britt said in a statement that “for too long, countries have used aggressive incentives to lure American production companies, and the jobs that come with them, overseas. This bipartisan legislation would level the playing field and reward companies for bringing production back home. I’m proud to join my colleagues in this effort.” Durbin said, “We should be doing everything we can to ensure that these productions stay in the United States rather than move overseas to take advantage of more competitive incentives.” If the bill doesn’t pass during the lame duck, it will have to be reintroduced in the next Congress. Figures like Durbin and Tillis are retiring, while other co-sponsors, like Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) and Rep. Thomas Kean Jr. (R-NJ) lost their seats in the midterms. That said, Congress could be led by two Democrats from a major production hub, New York, if Hakeem Jeffries is elected House speaker and Schumer is selected as Senate majority leader. The House version of the bill now has 76 cosponsors and the Senate version has 1 4. title: UK Culture Minister Delivers Emotional Plea To YouTube To “Set An Example” & Remove Russell Brand’s Channel
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Biggest ITV Shows Like ‘Love Island’ & ‘I’m A Celebrity’ To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of “Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States” On UK Audiences Melissa George Leading BBC-BritBox Detective Series ‘The Loch Ness Mysteries’ View All November 19, 2026 3:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ian Murray (left) Angeles Rodenas The UK government minister responsible for film and TV has made a personal plea to YouTube to “set an example” and remove Russell Brand ’s channel. Earlier, and under pressure, the Google-owned behemoth said it was investigating the video in which Brand’s wife Laura protested his innocence via a statement he sent her from prison. The UK government has previously called this video “appalling” and YouTube said it was investigating at the same time as Murray was speaking at the British Screen Forum Conference in London. Related Stories News Senate And House Lawmakers Added As Cosponsors To New Federal Film & TV Incentive Legislation News YouTube Investigating Russell Brand Prison Message Video “They would have taken it down if it was a mass murderer so please take it down,” implored Murray. “They are refusing to do so but could set an example.” Watch on Deadline A Google spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.” Murray said the Brand scandal has “highlighted what we’ve known going all the way back to the proliferation of these cases.” “It’s morally repugnant that we are still having these discussions today when we’ve been having them for 25 to 30 years,” he added. “I plead with everyone to sort it out and make everyone safe.” Some are calling on the UK government to intervene with legislation but Murray stressed the problem goes beyond this and needs the industry as a whole to take action. His boss, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, convened a meeting of industry leaders earlier this week after Brand was sentenced to 10 years in prison and following the David Walliams allegations, which Walliams denies. “It’s gone on for too long,” added Murray. “We are ruining people’s lives. It shouldn’t take brave women to come forward for something to be done about this.” UK considering implications of U.S. tax incentive Elsewhere, the UK government is keeping a firm eye on the proposed U.S. federal tax incentive for film and TV, added Murray. Murray said “we take the implications incredibly seriously” of the proposed 20% credit, which Donald Trump just gave his full-throated backing. He stressed that the outcome “remains to be seen.” Murray didn’t elaborate on his concerns but presumably fears the UK could lose production to America if the credit gets rubberstamped. With its own tax credit introduced more than a decade ago, the UK has become quite the hub for American projects, attracing millions of dollars each year. Huge movies like Wicked and Barbie have shot in Britain in recent years. Murray said: “This is a healthy sector but it’s fragile, so we are working closely with industry supporting a stronger domestic sector while welcoming inwards investment and the benefit that brings.” In September, the first-of-its-kind tax credit was introduced by a bipartisan group of lawmakers to create a 20% federal film and TV incentive, which is designed to lure production back to the U.S. Earlier this week, Trump lent his backing , saying meetings are being set up with leaders of both parties to “get this done!” Government “fundamentally rejects prospect of smaller BBC” Murray and his team are in the process of negotiating a new charter with the BBC and he said today the government’s white paper in the area is coming soon. He was vociferous in his backing for allowing the BBC to “survive and thrive,” noting that the government “fundamentally rejects the prospect of a smaller BBC,” while urging the industry to be more public in supporting the nation’s 100-year-old broadcaster. “We lose it at our peril,” said Murray. “If we value it we must vocally say that we back it. That’s my plea to you this morning.” With a new version of BBC iPlayer currently being tested, Murray said it should be the “world’s leading platform for video delivery” and should be “democratized.” New DG Matt Brittin has previously spoken of a YouTube-style “public service algorithm” connected to iPlayer. Murray was speaking at the British Screen Forum in London. Later will be keynotes from BBC deputy boss Rhodri Talfan Davies and Ken Loach’s producing partner Rebecca O’Brien. title: BeIN Media Group To Bring ‘Michael’, ‘Hamnet’ & ‘Jurassic World Rebirth’ To MENA Audiences With Fresh NBC Universal Deal

The deal with NBCUniversal Global TV Distribution , announced on the sidelines of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar’s Doha Industry Days 2026, gives beIN exclusive rights to a broad portfolio of NBCUniversal content across the Middle East and North Africa ( MENA ), including Pay-1 films and first-run series. The deal will provide high-end content for beIN’s entertainment channels, beIN ON DEMAND, beIN CONNECT, and TOD by beIN. Related Stories News Qatar's Film Committee & UAE-Based Yango Play Explore Partnership Kicking Off With Falconry Doc Series 'Elzam' Festivals Qatar's Film Committee Head Hassan Al-Thawadi Teases 2nd Industry Days In Doha: "We Are moving From Vision To Execution" It covers regional rights to NBCUniversal’s latest films following their theatrical release, as well as new series premiering for the first time in the region, Peacock Original content, and a vast collection of NBCUniversal’s beloved library film and TV series. Watch on Deadline As well as Michael , Jurassic World Rebirth , and Hamnet , the deal also includes The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, and Wicked: For Good as well as movies from the franchises Fast & Furious, How to Train Your Dragon , Minions , Shrek, and Downton Abbey . Dramas series covered by the accord include recently released legal drama War , starring Sienna Miller Dominic West, as well as the complete sets of library shows such as The Office and Suits “This agreement represents an important addition to beIN’s entertainment portfolio across MENA by further strengthening the depth and breadth of premium content available to our subscribers, whenever and wherever they want,” said Esra Özaral Altop, Group Chief Entertainment Officer, beIN Media Group. Michael Bonner, President, NBCUniversal Global TV Distribution added that the new agreement builds on the studio’s on existing “valued” relationship with beIN and also showed their shared commitment to bring high-end content to audiences across the Middle East and North Africa. “With beIN’s reach and deep understanding of the region, we look forward to continuing our work together and offering their viewers an exceptional range of NBCUniversal films and television series for years to come,” he said. title: Qatar’s Film Committee & UAE-Based Yango Play Explore Partnership Kicking Off With Falconry Doc Series ‘Elzam’
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie BeIN Media Group To Bring ‘Michael’, ‘Hamnet’ & ‘Jurassic World Rebirth’ To MENA Audiences With Fresh NBCUniversal Deal Netflix Unveils Penélope Cruz & Juan Diego Botto’s Domestic Violence Drama ‘Patricia’ As Production Gets Underway Qatar’s Film Committee Head Hassan Al-Thawadi Teases 2nd Industry Days In Doha: “We Are Moving From Vision To Execution” View All November 19, 2026 4:59am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Elzam Katara Studios The Film Committee at Media City Qatar has signed a memorandum of understanding with UAE-based regional streaming service Yango Play to explore the development, co-production and distribution of scripted and unscripted Arabic-language originals. The accord, announced on the sidelines of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar’s Doha Industry Days 2026, will also cover content acquisition and licensing opportunities, kicking off with eight-part Qatari documentary series Elzam . Produced by Doha-based Katara Studios, the series explores the Gulf region tradition of falconry through a group of contemporary falconers. It with premiere with the screening of a special episode at the Doha Film Festival , running alongside the Industry Days.
